title: Our closest cousins: what we share with the other apes, and whether humans are special

summary.text: Until 1960, books said that making tools was the thing that made us human. Then a chimpanzee in Tanzania pulled the leaves off a stem and used the stem to fish for termites. So what is left that only humans do? In this lesson you make three termite fishing tools from curry-leaf stalks and test which one catches the most. You also write your own list of things only humans can do, and check each one against what scientists have seen other apes do.
summary.art: A child poking a curry-leaf stalk into a plastic bottle of sesame seeds, beside a small drawing of a chimpanzee poking a stem into a termite mound in the same way.

intro.hook: A chimpanzee picks a stem, pulls off the leaves and pushes the stem into a termite mound. Is that a tool? Did the chimpanzee make it? And if a chimpanzee can make a tool, what can only a human do?
intro.text: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives. For a long time, people kept a list of things that only humans do: make tools, have culture, know themselves, care about others. In this lesson you write your own list first. Then you test a tool the way a chimpanzee makes one, and you look at the evidence for each thing on the list. Some things come off the list. Some are still argued about. You decide what stays.
intro.art: A notebook page headed 'Only humans can...' with six blank lines, a pencil beside it, and a curry-leaf stalk lying across the corner of the page.

outcomes: By the end I can say where humans sit in the ape family, and what a common ancestor is.
By the end I can explain what 'almost 99 per cent the same DNA' means, and what the joined chromosome shows.
By the end I can describe how chimpanzees make tools, using my results from the Termite Fishing Test.
By the end I can say what culture is, and how scientists tell a learned tradition from genes or from the place.
By the end I can give evidence that other apes feel, remember and understand others, and say what is still argued about.
By the end I can tell how Jane Goodall found out what she did, and why patient watching changed science.
By the end I can argue, with evidence, about whether humans are special, and say what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: A primate is a member of the group of mammals that includes lorises, lemurs, monkeys and apes. Most primates have hands that grip, nails in place of claws, and eyes that face forward.
terms.example: A bonnet macaque on a temple wall in Madurai is a primate. So is the person feeding the macaque.
terms.art: A bonnet macaque and a girl sitting on the same low wall, each holding a banana in a gripping hand.

terms.meaning: An ape is a primate with no tail and with shoulders that let the arms swing in a full circle. Gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans are apes.
terms.example: Swing your arm round like a bowler in cricket. A monkey's shoulder does not turn that far, but an ape's shoulder does.
terms.art: A girl bowling a cricket ball with her arm high, beside a gibbon hanging from a branch by one long arm.

terms.meaning: The great apes are the large apes: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans. Biologists put all of them in one family.
terms.example: A gibbon is an ape but not a great ape. A gibbon is much smaller, so gibbons are called small apes.
terms.art: Five figures in a row seen from behind: an orangutan, a gorilla, a chimpanzee, a bonobo and a human child.

terms.meaning: A common ancestor is a living being from long ago from whom two kinds of living beings today both descend.
terms.example: You and your cousin share a grandmother. Humans and chimpanzees share ancestors who lived about 6 to 8 million years ago. Those ancestors were neither humans nor chimpanzees.
terms.art: A simple tree with one trunk splitting into two branches, a human at the tip of one and a chimpanzee at the tip of the other, with a question-mark figure at the fork.

terms.meaning: DNA is the long molecule inside almost every cell that stores the instructions for building and running a living being. The instructions are written in four chemical letters: A, T, C and G.
terms.example: One set of human DNA has about 3,000 million letters. A chimpanzee's DNA is about the same length.
terms.art: A twisted ladder of DNA with its rungs labelled A, T, C and G.

terms.meaning: A chromosome is one long piece of DNA, wound up tightly. The DNA in a cell is divided into many chromosomes.
terms.example: A human cell has 46 chromosomes. A chimpanzee, gorilla or orangutan cell has 48.
terms.art: A row of X-shaped chromosomes of different sizes, with one long one circled.

terms.meaning: A tool is an object that a living being picks up and uses to get a job done. Making a tool means changing the object so that it does the job better.
terms.example: A stem lying on the ground is not a tool. A stem with the leaves pulled off, pushed into a termite mound to catch termites, is a tool that someone made.
terms.art: A leafy stem, then the same stem stripped bare, then the bare stem with termites holding on to its tip.

terms.meaning: A tool set is two or more different tools used one after the other for one job.
terms.example: Chimpanzees in the Goualougo forest in the Republic of Congo carry a thick stick to make a hole in a termite nest. Then they use a thin stem with a brush tip to fish.
terms.art: A chimpanzee holding a thick stick in one hand and a thin stem with a frayed tip in the mouth, beside a termite mound.

terms.meaning: A brush tip is the end of a stem that has been split into many thin fibres, like a paintbrush.
terms.example: Goualougo chimpanzees pull the end of a stem through their teeth to fray it. More termites hold on to the frayed end.
terms.art: A close view of a stem end split into many fine fibres, with small termites gripping the fibres.

terms.meaning: Social learning is learning something from others, by watching them or being with them, and not only by working it out alone.
terms.example: You learned to eat with your hand, or with a spoon, by watching your family. A young chimpanzee learns to crack nuts by watching the mother for years.
terms.art: A small child watching her grandmother shape a dosa on a tawa, with a young chimpanzee watching a mother crack a nut in a second panel.

terms.meaning: A tradition is a way of doing something that members of a group learn from each other and keep doing over time.
terms.example: Drawing a kolam at the door each morning is a tradition. Cracking nuts with a stone is a tradition of the chimpanzees of the Taï forest.
terms.art: A woman drawing a kolam at a doorstep while a girl copies a smaller one beside her.

terms.meaning: Culture is the whole set of traditions that a group has. Scientists say a group of animals has culture when the group's learned traditions differ from those of other groups of the same species.
terms.example: Chimpanzees at Taï crack nuts and chimpanzees at Gombe do not, though Gombe has nuts and stones. The difference is learned, so it is part of each group's culture.
terms.art: A map of Africa with two forests marked, one showing a chimpanzee cracking a nut and the other a chimpanzee fishing for termites.

terms.meaning: Cumulative culture is culture that builds up. Each generation learns what the last one knew and then adds to it, so skills become too complicated for one person to invent alone.
terms.example: No one person invented the bicycle from nothing. Wheels, metal working, chains and rubber tyres were each worked out by different people over thousands of years.
terms.art: A row of objects growing more complicated from left to right: a log roller, a wooden cart wheel, a bicycle.

terms.meaning: To imitate is to copy the actions that someone else does.
terms.example: A child who watches an aunt tie a sari and then makes the same folds in the same order is imitating her.
terms.art: A girl copying the hand movements of an older woman who is folding cloth.

terms.meaning: A gesture is a movement of the hand, arm or body that is made to tell another being something.
terms.example: You hold out your hand, palm up, to ask for a share of a mango. A chimpanzee makes the same gesture to ask for food.
terms.art: A child's open hand held out palm up, and a chimpanzee's open hand held out in the same way.

terms.meaning: The mirror test checks whether an animal knows that the reflection in a mirror is their own body. A mark is put where the animal can see it only in the mirror.
terms.example: A chimpanzee with a spot of dye on the eyebrow looks in the mirror and then touches their own eyebrow. That shows the chimpanzee knows whose face it is.
terms.art: A chimpanzee looking into a mirror and touching a red mark above their own eye.

terms.meaning: A field study is research done where the animals live, by watching them for a long time without controlling what they do.
terms.example: The study of the chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania began in 1960 and is still going on.
terms.art: A woman sitting quietly on a hillside with binoculars and a notebook, with chimpanzees in the trees below.

terms.meaning: A species is endangered when so few are left that the species could die out.
terms.example: Every kind of great ape except humans is endangered. India's only ape, the hoolock gibbon, is endangered too.
terms.art: A hoolock gibbon sitting high in a lone tree, with tea gardens and a road on both sides.

explanations.concept: Humans are apes: where we sit in the family
explanations.definition: Apes are primates without tails. The great apes are orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans. Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, and we are theirs.
explanations.description: People often say 'apes and humans', as if these were two groups. Biologists do not sort them that way. They sort living beings by who shares the most recent common ancestor, in the way you are closer to your sister than to your cousin. By that rule, humans are inside the great ape family. Here is the surprising part. A chimpanzee is more closely related to you than to a gorilla. The line that led to gorillas split off first. The line that led to humans and the line that led to chimpanzees and bonobos stayed together for longer. They split about 6 to 8 million years ago. The dates come from counting DNA differences and from fossils, and scientists still adjust them. Humans did not come from chimpanzees. Both came from ancestors who were neither. Since the split, both lines have gone on changing for the same length of time. So a chimpanzee is not an 'earlier' or 'unfinished' human. A chimpanzee is as up to date as you are.
examples: Orangutans split off first among the great apes, then gorillas. The last split was between the human line and the line of chimpanzees and bonobos.
Chimpanzees and bonobos split from each other much later, perhaps 1 to 2 million years ago. So we are exactly as closely related to bonobos as to chimpanzees.
Gibbons, the small apes, split off before all the great apes. The hoolock gibbon of Assam and other north-eastern states is India's only ape.

In 2015, a 13-million-year-old tooth of a small ape was found at Ramnagar in Jammu and Kashmir. Scientists named the ape Kapi ramnagarensis in 2020. They think this ape was an early relative of gibbons. It is only one tooth, so they are careful about it.
explanations.art: A branching tree with gibbons splitting off first, then orangutans, then gorillas, and a last fork leading to humans on one side and to chimpanzees and bonobos on the other.

explanations.concept: What 'almost 99 per cent the same DNA' really means
explanations.definition: When scientists line up human DNA and chimpanzee DNA letter by letter, about 99 letters in every 100 are the same. The exact number depends on what is counted.
explanations.description: In 2005 scientists published the first reading of nearly all of a chimpanzee's DNA, and compared it with human DNA. Where the two could be lined up letter by letter, they differed at about 1.2 letters in every 100. That is where 'almost 99 per cent the same' comes from. But there is a second kind of difference. In some places, a stretch of letters is present in one species and missing in the other. If you count those stretches too, the two are about 96 per cent the same. In 2025 scientists finished reading ape DNA from end to end, including the hardest parts. They found some regions so rearranged that they cannot be lined up letter by letter at all. So there is no single true number. The honest answer is 'very alike, and how alike depends on how you count'. Why does a small difference in letters give such different bodies? One reason is that 1.2 in 100 is still about 35 million letters. Another is that some DNA works like a switch. A switch decides when and where a gene is used, and for how long. Many scientists think that changes in switches, more than changes in the genes themselves, explain why our bodies and brains grow differently.
examples: Two humans picked from anywhere on Earth differ at about 1 letter in every 1,000. A human and a chimpanzee differ about ten times more than that.
About 35 million single letters differ between a human and a chimpanzee. About 5 million more places have a stretch that is added or missing.
In the Hundred Square activity, you colour 1 square in 100 for letters that differ, and 3 more for stretches that are added or missing.
The same DNA comparison works for any two living beings. The more recent their common ancestor, the more alike their DNA.
explanations.art: A grid of 100 small squares with one square coloured red and three coloured blue, beside two long rows of DNA letters with one differing letter circled.

explanations.definition: Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans have 48 chromosomes in each cell. Humans have 46. Human chromosome 2 is two ancestral chromosomes joined end to end.
explanations.description: If humans and other great apes share ancestors, the different chromosome numbers need explaining. Scientists made a guess that could be tested. Perhaps two chromosomes joined into one on the human line, some time after the split. If that is true, the join should have left marks. Every chromosome has special repeated letters at each end, like the plastic tips on a shoelace. Each also has one pinched-in place, used when a cell divides. A joined chromosome should have end letters in its middle, where no ends belong. It should also have the remains of a second pinched-in place. In 1991, Jacob Ijdo and his team found end letters in the middle of human chromosome 2. In 1992, another team found the faded remains of a second pinched-in place. The DNA on either side matches two separate chimpanzee chromosomes. A guess that could have failed did not fail. That is strong evidence that we share ancestors with the other great apes.
examples: In the Joined Chromosome activity you tape two paper strips end to end, and predict what marks the join should leave.
The two chimpanzee chromosomes that match our chromosome 2 are now called 2A and 2B.
The join did not remove any genes. It only changed how the same DNA is packed.
explanations.art: Two short striped chromosomes with coloured tips above, and one long chromosome below made of the same two stripe patterns, with the coloured tips meeting in its middle.

explanations.concept: Same plan, different measurements: ape bodies
explanations.definition: All apes are built from the same parts in the same order. Humans differ from other apes mainly in the sizes and shapes of those parts.
explanations.description: A chimpanzee's hand has the same bones as yours, with nails and fingerprints. A chimpanzee has the same teeth as you, in the same number. The differences are measurements. Human legs are long and human arms are short, because we walk upright on two legs. A chimpanzee's arms are longer than their legs, which suits climbing and walking on the knuckles. Human thumbs are longer, so a human thumb tip can press firmly against each fingertip. Human bodies have thin, short hair and many sweat glands, so we cool down well on a long walk in the sun. The human brain is about three times as big as a chimpanzee's. Each body suits a way of living. Many people think a chimpanzee is five or more times as strong as a person. Careful tests give a smaller number. In 2017 a team led by Matthew O'Neill measured chimpanzee muscle. They found it gives about 1.35 times the force and power of human muscle of the same size. Chimpanzee muscle has more fast fibres, which are strong but tire quickly. Human muscle has more slow fibres, which keep going. Our bodies gave up some power for staying power.
examples: Press your thumb tip against the tip of your little finger. A chimpanzee's shorter thumb and longer fingers make this grip harder.
A chimpanzee's big toe sticks out sideways and grips like a thumb. Your big toe lines up with the others, which helps you push off when you walk.
A gorilla's large belly holds a long gut for digesting leaves and stems all day.
An orangutan's arms can span more than 2 metres from fingertip to fingertip, for reaching between branches.
explanations.art: A human skeleton and a chimpanzee skeleton standing side by side at the same height, with matching bones in the arm and hand shaded the same colour.

explanations.concept: Tools: what Jane Goodall saw, and what came after
explanations.definition: Chimpanzees, orangutans and some other animals use tools. Chimpanzees also make tools, by changing an object so that it does a job better.
explanations.description: In the autumn of 1960, at Gombe in Tanzania, Jane Goodall watched a chimpanzee she called David Greybeard. He pushed a grass stem into a termite mound, pulled it out and ate the termites holding on to it. Later she saw chimpanzees pick leafy twigs and strip the leaves off first. Stripping the leaves is the important part. It means the chimpanzee changed an object to fit a job. That is making a tool, and scientists at that time said only humans did it. Since then, watchers at other sites have found much more. At Goualougo in the Republic of Congo, chimpanzees fray the end of a stem into a brush. In 2009 Crickette Sanz and her team asked five local guides to fish at real termite nests with both kinds of stem. The brush tips brought out about 5 termites each try. The plain stems brought out about one termite in every four tries. In the Termite Fishing Test, you check whether a frayed tip also works better for you. At Fongoli in Senegal, chimpanzees sharpen sticks with their teeth and jab them into tree holes to hunt small animals called bushbabies. Jill Pruetz, who studies them, found that females hunted with these tools more than males did.
examples: Termite fishing with a stripped stem, first seen at Gombe in Tanzania in 1960.
Brush-tipped fishing stems and tool sets at Goualougo in the Republic of Congo.
Stone and wooden hammers for cracking nuts at Taï in Ivory Coast. Stones found there show that chimpanzees were cracking nuts 4,300 years ago.
Sponges of chewed leaves for soaking up water from tree holes, at Budongo in Uganda and elsewhere.
Tools are not only for apes. On Great Nicobar Island, Indian scientists led by Arijit Pal saw long-tailed macaques wrap and wipe food, and clean between their teeth with threads and fibres.
explanations.art: A chimpanzee sitting by a termite mound, pulling a thin stem out of a hole, with several termites clinging to the end of the stem.

explanations.concept: Culture: learned traditions that differ from group to group
explanations.definition: Culture is a group's set of traditions, learned from each other. Chimpanzee and orangutan groups have cultures.
explanations.description: How can anyone tell that a habit is learned from others? In 1999 Andrew Whiten and scientists from seven long-running chimpanzee studies put their records together. They listed every behaviour that was common in at least one group and missing in another. Then they removed two kinds of difference. If a group had no termite mounds, then 'no termite fishing' was caused by the place, so they removed it. All the groups were chimpanzees, so differences in genes could not easily explain a habit found in one group and missing next door. After that, 39 behaviours were left. These included ways of using tools, of grooming and of courting. Each group had their own mix, as each human community does. In 2003 Carel van Schaik's team did the same for orangutans and found 24. Culture can also be watched as it spreads. In 2011 at Budongo in Uganda, Catherine Hobaiter filmed a new habit, a sponge made of moss, as it passed from one chimpanzee to another. Almost every chimpanzee who made a moss sponge had first watched another make one. The story in this lesson tells what she saw.
examples: Taï chimpanzees crack nuts with hammers. Gombe chimpanzees have nuts and stones but do not crack nuts.
At Mahale in Tanzania, two chimpanzees who groom each other often clasp hands above their heads. Most other groups do not.

In 1953 on Koshima island in Japan, a young macaque named Imo began washing sweet potatoes in water. Others learned it from her. Japanese scientists led by Kinji Imanishi had already suggested in 1952 that monkeys could have culture.
In the game Learned, Place or Genes? you sort differences between groups in the way Whiten's team did.
explanations.art: Two groups of chimpanzees on either side of a river, one group cracking nuts on stones and the other clasping hands overhead while grooming.

explanations.concept: How young apes learn: years of watching
explanations.definition: Young apes learn their group's skills over many years, mostly by watching their mothers closely and practising.
explanations.description: A young chimpanzee stays close to the mother for years. The young one watches her fish, crack nuts and choose food, from a hand's width away. Cracking a nut looks easy. In fact it needs three things placed just right: the nut, a flat stone or root under it, and a hammer of the right weight. Hit too softly and nothing happens. Hit too hard and the nut is crushed. Young chimpanzees at Taï take years to get good at it, and do not reach an adult's skill until they are grown. You can feel why in the Hammer and Anvil activity. Do chimpanzee mothers teach? Mostly they let the young watch, and they put up with the young taking their tools and their nuts. Christophe Boesch, who has studied the Taï chimpanzees for decades, reported in 1991 that he twice saw a mother clearly show her child how to do it. Two clear cases in many years is very few. So scientists argue about how much teaching other apes do. Humans teach all the time. Humans also copy in a special way, which you can test in the Copycat Test.
examples: An orangutan child stays with the mother for about seven or eight years, learning which of hundreds of plants to eat and how to build a nest.
At Taï, a young chimpanzee often uses the mother's own hammer, and does better with it.
In a test in 2005, young chimpanzees who could see that a step did nothing left it out. Children of three and four copied every step.
explanations.art: A young chimpanzee sitting very close to her mother, eyes on the mother's hands as the mother lifts a stone over a nut on a flat root.

explanations.definition: Other apes form close bonds that last for life. They comfort each other, grieve, make up after fights and care for the hurt.
explanations.description: Other apes feel. The evidence is in what they do, and it has been collected for more than sixty years. At Gombe in 1972, an old mother named Flo died. Her young son Flint stayed near the place, stopped eating, grew weak and died about three weeks later. After a fight, two chimpanzees often come back together, hold out a hand, embrace and groom. Frans de Waal, who first studied this making up, also saw a third chimpanzee put an arm round the loser of a fight. Apes look after wounds. In June 2022 in Sumatra, a male orangutan named Rakus had a wound on his face. Scientists watched him chew the leaves of a climbing plant that local people use as medicine. He put the juice on the wound and then covered it with the chewed leaves. The wound closed in five days. Nobody knows whether Rakus worked this out alone or learned it from others. These are the same kinds of acts that show feeling in a person who cannot speak, such as a baby. Some scientists say we should describe only the acts and not name the feeling. That view is given in the challenging views.
examples: A chimpanzee mother may carry her dead baby for days or weeks.
At Taï, adult chimpanzees, including males, have adopted young orphans and shared food with them for years.
Young chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans all laugh when tickled.
Grooming a friend takes up hours of a chimpanzee's day. It cleans the hair, and it keeps friendships strong.
explanations.art: An adult chimpanzee with one arm round the shoulders of another who sits hunched after a fight.

explanations.concept: What goes on in an ape's mind: memory, self and other minds
explanations.definition: Other apes remember, plan, know themselves in a mirror and keep track of what others can see and know. In some tasks they do better than humans.
explanations.description: In 1970 Gordon Gallup gave some chimpanzees a mirror for several days. Then, while they were asleep under a vet's medicine, he put a spot of dye on one eyebrow. When they woke and looked in the mirror, they touched the spot on their own faces. They knew whose face they were seeing. In 2007 in Japan, Sana Inoue and Tetsuro Matsuzawa showed a young chimpanzee named Ayumu five numbers on a screen for about a fifth of a second. Then the numbers were covered. Ayumu touched the places in the right order about 8 times in 10. University students given the same task did much worse at that speed. Later, other scientists showed that people who practise a great deal can match Ayumu. So the test shows two things. A chimpanzee's memory for a quick glance is very good, and practice matters for everyone. Do apes know what another is thinking? In 2016 Christopher Krupenye and his team showed films to chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans. In the films, a person saw an object hidden, and it was moved while the person was away. A camera followed the apes' eyes. Most of them looked at the place where the person wrongly thought the object was. That suggests they kept track of what the person believed. Scientists still argue about how far this goes.
examples: In the One Glance activity, you take a paper form of Ayumu's test.
All five orangutans in a 2007 test got a groundnut out of a tall tube by carrying water in their mouths and spitting it in, so the nut floated up.
When children were given the same floating nut test in 2011, about 1 in 12 four-year-olds and about 6 in 10 eight-year-olds found the answer.
Chimpanzees remember where fruit trees are, and seem to plan routes to reach them early.
explanations.art: A young chimpanzee touching white squares on a screen, with the hidden numbers 1 to 5 shown faintly inside the squares.

explanations.concept: Gestures, calls and the language question
explanations.definition: Other apes talk to each other with gestures, calls, faces and touch. Whether any of this, or anything apes have been taught, counts as language is still argued about.
explanations.description: Wild chimpanzees use dozens of gestures on purpose. The gesturer looks at the other, waits for an answer, and tries again if nothing happens. Catherine Hobaiter and her team have worked out what many of the gestures ask for. An open hand held out asks for food. A long, loud scratch on one's own arm asks to be groomed there. In 2023 Kirsty Graham and Catherine Hobaiter showed films of chimpanzee and bonobo gestures to 5,656 people online. Each person chose one meaning out of four. By chance they would be right 1 time in 4. They were right more than half the time. So we still understand much of our cousins' sign system. From the 1960s, scientists also tried to teach apes human signs and symbols. A gorilla named Koko and a bonobo named Kanzi learned hundreds. What that shows is argued about.
examples: In the Talking Without Words activity, your family guesses messages from hands and body alone.
A chimpanzee who finds a snake gives an alarm call, and calls more when others nearby have not seen the snake yet.
Human babies point to show things to others before they can talk. Other apes seldom point just to share something interesting.

perspectives.who: Scientists who taught signs and symbols to apes, such as Francine Patterson and Sue Savage-Rumbaugh
perspectives.explanation: The apes used hundreds of signs or symbols to ask, answer and name things, and understood many spoken requests. That is the beginning of language.

perspectives.who: Herbert Terrace, who taught signs to a chimpanzee named Nim
perspectives.explanation: After studying his own films, he concluded in 1979 that Nim mostly copied his teachers and strung signs together to get rewards, without grammar. Language needs grammar.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study wild apes, such as Catherine Hobaiter
perspectives.explanation: Asking whether apes can learn our language is the wrong test. Their own gestures and calls already carry meaning, and that is what should be studied.

explanations.art: Two chimpanzees facing each other, one holding out an open hand palm up, the other looking at the hand.

explanations.concept: Chimpanzees and bonobos: fighting, hunting, sharing and peace
explanations.definition: Our two closest relatives live differently. Chimpanzee groups are led by males and can be violent to neighbours. Bonobo groups are led by females and are more peaceful, though not always.
explanations.description: At first Jane Goodall thought chimpanzees were gentler than people. Then she and the Gombe field staff saw two things that shocked her. Chimpanzees hunt monkeys in groups and eat the meat. And from 1974 to 1978, the Gombe chimpanzees split into two groups, and the males of one group killed the males of the other, one at a time. Chimpanzees also share meat, adopt orphans and comfort the hurt. Both are true of the same animals. Bonobos live only south of the Congo River. Among bonobos, females stick together and outrank the males, and neighbouring groups sometimes meet and mix peacefully. Bonobos do fight, but killings like those at Gombe are almost unknown among them. Nobody is sure why the two species differ. We are equally related to both. So nobody can point to chimpanzees and say 'humans are violent by nature', or to bonobos and say 'humans are peaceful by nature'.
examples: Chimpanzee males patrol the edge of their range in silent single file.
Bonobo females who are not related still groom each other, share food and back each other up against males.
After a hunt, a chimpanzee holding meat is surrounded by others holding out open hands. Many are given a piece.
explanations.art: A split picture: on one side a line of male chimpanzees walking silently along a forest path, on the other a group of bonobo females sitting close and sharing fruit.

explanations.concept: How we know: watching for years, and who did the watching
explanations.definition: Almost everything known about wild apes comes from field studies in which people watch the same individuals, by name, for many years.
explanations.description: Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe on 14 July 1960, aged 26, with her mother Vanne. The officials would not let a young woman camp there alone. She had no university degree. For months the chimpanzees ran from her. She kept coming back to the same hillside until they stopped running. She gave them names such as David Greybeard, Flo and Fifi, and wrote about their different characters. When she went to Cambridge University to study for a doctorate, some scientists told her this was wrong. They said animals should have numbers, and that only humans have personalities. She did not agree, and in time most scientists came round to her view. She was not the only one working this way. Japanese scientists had been naming individual monkeys since the 1950s. Dian Fossey with gorillas and Biruté Galdikas with orangutans began long studies soon after. And much of the Gombe record was written by Tanzanians. Hilali Matama was hired in 1968, one of the first Tanzanian research assistants. Today Tanzanian field staff follow the chimpanzees and collect the data every day. Jane Goodall died on 1 October 2025, aged 91. The Gombe study still goes on.
examples: A single visit could never have shown the four-year fight between two groups, or a mother's skills passing to her daughter.
Naming individuals lets a watcher follow one life for decades: who their mother was, whom they learned from, and whom they trusted.
Louis Leakey, who sent Jane Goodall to Gombe, also helped Dian Fossey and Biruté Galdikas begin.
explanations.art: A young woman with a notebook sitting on a grassy ridge above a forest at dawn, and in a second panel, a Tanzanian man with a clipboard following a chimpanzee along a forest path.

explanations.definition: Humans share tool making, culture, feelings, memory and self-knowledge with other apes. What, if anything, is found only in humans is still argued about.
explanations.description: Look at what has come off the old list: tools, culture, knowing yourself in a mirror, comforting a friend. Each was once called 'only human'. Each was then seen in other apes by someone who watched long enough. Some things have not been seen in other apes. No other ape has a language with grammar that can say anything at all. No other ape's culture builds up and up, so that a child today uses tools no single person could invent. No other ape cooks food, or works together in groups of thousands of strangers. Are these new kinds of things, or the same things grown larger? Scientists disagree, and their main views are below. There is one more thing to notice. 'Special' can mean 'different from the others'. In that sense every species is special. A chimpanzee beats us at glance memory, a gibbon at swinging, an orangutan at knowing a thousand forest plants. 'Special' can also mean 'above the others'. Science has no test for that meaning.
examples: In the Copycat Test, you find out whether people copy a step that clearly does nothing. Some scientists think this habit of exact copying is what lets human culture build up.
In the game Only Humans?, you sort sixteen claims into 'others do it too', 'still argued about' and 'not seen in other apes so far'.
Other kinds of humans, such as Neanderthals, lived until about 40,000 years ago. If they were still here, the gap between us and our nearest relatives would look smaller.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, in The Descent of Man (1871)
perspectives.explanation: The difference in mind between humans and other animals is great, but it is a difference of degree and not of kind. Other animals have the same abilities in smaller amounts.

perspectives.who: Thomas Suddendorf, a psychologist, in The Gap (2013)
perspectives.explanation: There is a real gap. Two things widen it: humans can imagine endless possible situations and think about them, and humans have a strong urge to share what is in their minds with others.

perspectives.who: Michael Tomasello, who has compared young children and other apes for many years
perspectives.explanation: Other apes are clever alone. What humans add is doing things together with a shared goal: pointing things out, teaching, and helping each other on a common task from a very young age.

perspectives.who: Frans de Waal, who studied chimpanzees and bonobos for most of his life
perspectives.explanation: Each time a line is drawn between humans and other animals, later evidence rubs it out. It is better to ask what each species is good at than to look for a line.

explanations.art: A child and a chimpanzee sitting side by side on a log, each looking at their own open hand.

explanations.concept: Our cousins are in danger, and so are their cultures
explanations.definition: Every great ape species except humans is endangered. When a group of apes is lost, the group's learned traditions are lost too.
explanations.description: Great apes have few young. A chimpanzee mother has one baby about every five years, and an orangutan mother one about every seven or eight. So a group that loses a few adults takes many years to recover. Forests are cut for farms, roads and mines. Apes are hunted, and babies are caught to be sold. There is a second kind of loss. In 2019 Hjalmar Kühl and a large team compared 144 chimpanzee communities and 31 behaviours. In places where people had changed the forest most, a behaviour was 88 per cent less likely to be found. A tradition needs enough chimpanzees, living close enough together, for the young to watch. When groups shrink and scatter, the watching stops. A tradition that is lost may not be invented again. This is why some scientists now say that ape cultures need protecting, and not only ape bodies. Some people also say that great apes should have a few basic rights in law, such as not being kept alone in a cage.
examples: The western hoolock gibbon, India's only ape, lives in forest patches cut apart by tea gardens, roads and railway lines. Gibbons seldom come down to the ground, so a gap in the trees can trap a family.
In 1999, New Zealand made a law that great apes may be used in research only when the research is for the good of the apes.
In 2016, a judge in Mendoza in Argentina ruled that a chimpanzee named Cecilia, who had lived in a zoo for more than 30 years, had some basic rights. Cecilia was moved to a sanctuary.

agreed.text: Humans, chimpanzees and bonobos descend from common ancestors, and chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives.
agreed.evidence: Their DNA is more like ours than any other species' DNA is. Human chromosome 2 carries the marks of two ape chromosomes joined end to end. Our bones, teeth, hands and blood are built on the same plan.
Jane Goodall saw it at Gombe in 1960. Since then it has been filmed at many sites, with stems, brush tips, sponges, stone hammers and sharpened sticks.

agreed.text: Groups of chimpanzees and orangutans have learned traditions that differ from group to group.
agreed.evidence: Records from seven long chimpanzee studies showed 39 behaviours that were common in some groups and missing in others, where the place could not explain the difference. In 2011 a new habit was filmed spreading among chimpanzees who had watched each other.

agreed.text: Great apes know their own bodies in a mirror.
agreed.evidence: Chimpanzees with a dye mark on the face touch the mark on their own face when they see a mirror. Gordon Gallup first showed this in 1970, and it has been repeated with orangutans, bonobos and some gorillas.

agreed.text: Other apes form bonds that last for years, and they act towards friends and family in ways that show feeling.
agreed.evidence: Long field studies have recorded mothers carrying dead babies, friends making up after fights, adults adopting orphans, and apes caring for wounds.

agreed.text: Every great ape species except humans is endangered.
agreed.evidence: The Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which counts wild populations, lists all of them as endangered or critically endangered.

challenging.who: Most scientists before 1960, who defined humans as 'Man the Toolmaker'
challenging.for: Nobody had reported a wild animal changing an object to fit a job. Human tools were found with the oldest human fossils known then.
challenging.against: In 1960 Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees strip leaves from twigs to fish for termites. Tool making has since been seen at many chimpanzee sites, and in orangutans and some birds.
challenging.context: This card is about an old definition of what makes us human. It was dropped after someone watched wild chimpanzees for long enough.

challenging.claim: Humans are the top of evolution, and other apes are less evolved.
challenging.who: A very common picture, drawn as a line of figures walking from a bent ape to an upright man
challenging.for: Humans have the largest brains for their body size, and have built cities, writing and machines.
challenging.against: Evolution is a branching tree and not a ladder. The chimpanzee line and the human line have been changing for exactly the same length of time since they split. Each fits their own way of living.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that living beings can be ranked from lower to higher. Biologists do not rank them this way.

challenging.claim: A scientist should give animals numbers and should never write about their feelings or characters.
challenging.who: Many scientists who studied animal behaviour in the 1960s
challenging.for: It is easy to imagine human feelings in an animal when they are not there. This mistake is called anthropomorphism. Numbers and plain descriptions guard against it.
challenging.against: Individual apes do differ in character, and those differences explain what happens in a group. Leaving them out makes the record less accurate. Most ape scientists now use names.
challenging.context: This card is about how scientists should write about animals. Jane Goodall was told that naming chimpanzees was unscientific.

challenging.claim: What chimpanzee groups have should not be called culture.
challenging.who: Some scientists, such as Claudio Tennie
challenging.for: Each chimpanzee might work the habit out alone, once the right things are around. Ape habits also stay simple. They do not build up over generations as human skills do.
challenging.against: At Budongo in 2011, a new moss sponge spread almost only to chimpanzees who had watched it being made. Groups living in similar forests keep different habits for decades.
challenging.context: This card is about the word 'culture'. Scientists agree that ape groups differ. They disagree about how the differences are learned and what to call them.

challenging.who: Scientists who taught signs or symbols to apes from the 1960s to the 1990s
challenging.for: Koko the gorilla and Kanzi the bonobo used hundreds of signs or symbols. Kanzi carried out many spoken requests he had never heard before.
challenging.against: Herbert Terrace found that the chimpanzee Nim mostly copied his teachers and repeated signs to get rewards. No taught ape has shown the grammar of even a three-year-old child.
challenging.context: This card is about whether an ape who is taught signs is using language. The scientists who did the teaching came to different answers.

challenging.claim: Human minds differ from other apes' minds in kind, and not only in amount.
challenging.who: Thomas Suddendorf and some other psychologists
challenging.for: No other ape has open-ended language, culture that builds up, or stories about the far past and future. These look like new abilities.
challenging.against: Charles Darwin and Frans de Waal argue that each of these grows out of something other apes have in a smaller amount, such as gestures, traditions and planning for tomorrow.
challenging.context: This card is about the biggest argument in this lesson: is the difference between humans and other apes one of amount, or one of kind?

big_questions.q: In the Termite Fishing Test you stripped the stalk before you fished. Where was the tool before you made it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you knew before your hands moved. Did David Greybeard need the same thing in his mind when he stripped a twig?

big_questions.q: Human and chimpanzee DNA can be called 99 per cent alike, or 96, or less. Can a question have one true answer if the counting rule is our choice?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Hundred Square. Nothing in the DNA changed between your counts. What changed?

big_questions.q: Ayumu the chimpanzee beats students at remembering a glance. Students beat Ayumu at sums. Is there one thing called intelligence?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one needs in daily life. What would a test written by a chimpanzee ask?

big_questions.q: People once said only humans make tools, and then that only humans have culture. Why did people want such a list at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a list like that lets people do to other animals. Think also about who was left out of the word 'Man' in 'Man the Toolmaker'.

big_questions.q: We are equally related to chimpanzees, who fight wars, and to bonobos, who mostly do not. What can their lives tell us about ourselves?
big_questions.hint: Two close relatives live very differently. Does that tell you more about what humans must be, or about what humans could be?

big_questions.q: A judge gave a chimpanzee named Cecilia some rights. What should decide who has rights: looking like us, thinking like us, or being able to feel?
big_questions.hint: Try each rule on a newborn baby, a chimpanzee, a crow and a fish. Which rule would you be willing to live under?

big_questions.q: When the last chimpanzees of a group die, their traditions end. Is something lost even if chimpanzees still live elsewhere?
big_questions.hint: Think of a language that only one village speaks. The people of the next village are alive. Is the language still a loss?

story.title: Who Was Watching Nick?
story.note: This is a true story. The forest, the date and time, the pool between the roots, the moss sponge, the six days, the second new habit and the count of sixty-eight chimpanzees are from the scientific report of 2014 by Catherine Hobaiter and her team. The sentence in quotation marks near the end is her own, from an interview. What Catherine thought and felt, and her evening with the films, are imagined. The names Nick and Nambi match the short codes NK and NB in the report. One radio report gives the alpha male's name as Mick.
text: The rains of 2011 were heavy in the Budongo Forest in Uganda. A river spilled over part of the forest floor. When the water went down, it left a small pool between the roots of two big trees.

Catherine Hobaiter knew every chimpanzee who came to drink there. She had followed this community, called Sonso, for years. Sixty-eight of them had names. She carried a notebook and a small video camera, and the chimpanzees took about as much notice of her as of a tree stump.

Sonso chimpanzees have one way of drinking from a pool like this. They pick a few leaves, fold them into the mouth and chew them into a wad. They dip the wad in the water and suck it like a sponge. Every grown chimpanzee at Sonso does this. Their mothers did it before them. In about twenty years of records, nobody had seen them do anything else.

On the morning of the fourteenth of November, at five minutes past nine, Nick walked up to the pool. Nick was the alpha male, the highest in rank. The others shifted out of his way. Catherine lifted the camera, as she did a hundred times a day.

Nick did not pick leaves. He reached to the trunk beside him and pulled off a handful of green moss. He rolled the moss loosely, put it in his mouth for a moment, took it out and pushed it into the water. Then he lifted it, dripping, and sucked.
Catherine held the camera very still. A sponge made of moss. In all the Sonso records, those words had never been written.

She was not the only one watching. Nambi, the highest-ranking female, sat an arm's length from Nick. Her eyes were on his hands. A little later Nambi pulled moss from the same trunk, rolled it and dipped it in the pool.

That evening Catherine watched the film again and again. One chimpanzee doing a new thing was interesting. Two was something else. If the moss sponge spread, she would be seeing what scientists had argued about for years.

The argument went like this. Chimpanzees in one forest crack nuts, and chimpanzees in another do not. Many scientists said this was culture: the young learn the habit by watching the old. Others were not sure. Perhaps each chimpanzee works the habit out alone, they said, when the right things happen to be lying around. To settle it, someone would have to catch a habit on the day it began. And for every chimpanzee who picked it up, that someone would have to know one thing. Had they watched another chimpanzee do it first?
Nobody had ever caught the first day in the wild. Catherine had the first day on film.
So from the next morning she wrote down more than who drank. For every visit to the pool she noted who was using what kind of sponge. And she noted who was sitting near enough to see.

The pool was a busy place that week. A young female named Karibu sat beside her mother, Kwera, while Kwera worked a lump of moss in the water. Karibu watched. Then Karibu reached for the trunk. One after another, over six days, seven more chimpanzees made moss sponges.

Each night Catherine went back through the films and asked her question. Before this chimpanzee's first moss sponge, had they watched someone make one? Yes. Yes. Yes. For six of the seven, the film showed them watching first.

Something else was new at the pool that week. Old leaf sponges lay on the ground all around it, dropped by earlier drinkers. A young male picked one up, chewed it and used it again. Soon others were doing the same. That was a new habit too. But when Catherine checked the films, these chimpanzees had not needed to watch anybody. Used sponges were everywhere. Anyone could come across one and try it.

So two new habits had started at one pool in one week. One of them turned up here and there, wherever a chimpanzee happened on an old sponge. The other moved like a message passed along a line, from the one who made it to the one who was looking.
And the chimpanzees who came to the pool that week but never saw a moss sponge being made? They went on folding leaves, as their mothers had.

Later Catherine and her team put every visit into a table and worked through the numbers. A chimpanzee who watched a moss sponge being made was about fifteen times more likely to start making one. Catherine said it more simply. 'Basically, if you saw it done, you learned how to do it, and if you didn't you didn't.'
Scientists checked again three years later. Moss sponges were still being made at Sonso.
Nick did not know he had begun anything. Nambi did not know she had passed anything on. Catherine knew, because she had written down who was drinking, and also who was watching.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the hidden idea is how scientists can tell that a habit is culture. It is not enough to see that a new habit appears. You must know, for each learner, whether they watched someone first. The moss sponge spread only along the lines of who watched whom. The reuse of old leaf sponges did not, because any chimpanzee could find an old sponge alone. That contrast, at one pool in one week, is the evidence. It also shows why patient watching and careful notes matter, as they did for Jane Goodall.
ask: Why was it not enough for Catherine to see that more and more chimpanzees were using moss?
Two new habits began at the pool that week. How were they different in the way they spread?
Suppose a chimpanzee had made a moss sponge without ever watching anyone. What would that tell you?
What did Catherine write down from the second morning that she had not written before? Why did it matter?
Think of something you do that you learned only by watching. Who was the person you watched?

games.title: Only Humans? The evidence cards
games.context: This is a card game about the list of things people once said only humans do. Each card makes one claim. You decide what the evidence says, then turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 16 claim cards to cut out (the evidence is on the back)

items.f: Only humans make tools.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. Chimpanzees strip twigs to fish for termites and fray stems into brushes. Jane Goodall saw the first case at Gombe in 1960.

items.f: Only humans have traditions that differ from one group to the next.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. In 1999 scientists counted 39 learned habits that some chimpanzee groups have and others lack. Orangutan groups differ too.

items.f: Only humans know their own face in a mirror.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. In 1970 chimpanzees with a dye mark on the eyebrow looked in a mirror and touched the mark on their own face.

items.f: Only humans comfort a friend who is upset.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. After a fight, a chimpanzee who took no part often puts an arm round the loser.

items.f: Only humans use plants as medicine.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. In 2022 an orangutan named Rakus chewed the leaves of a healing plant and put them on a wound on his face. The wound closed in five days.

items.f: Only humans make war on their neighbours.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. From 1974 to 1978 at Gombe, the males of one chimpanzee group killed the males of a neighbouring group, one by one.

items.f: Only humans laugh.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. Young chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans all laugh when they are tickled or chased in play.

items.f: Only humans can remember a set of numbers after one quick glance.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. A young chimpanzee named Ayumu did this better than university students in 2007. People who practise a lot can catch up.

items.f: Only humans ask for things with hand signals.
items.b: OTHERS DO IT TOO. Wild chimpanzees use dozens of gestures. An open hand asks for food. A loud scratch on the arm asks to be groomed there.

items.f: Only humans teach their young on purpose.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. Young apes mostly learn by watching. At Taï, a scientist twice saw a mother clearly show her child how to crack a nut. Two cases are very few.

items.f: Only humans know what someone else is thinking.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. In 2016 apes watching a film looked at the place where a person wrongly believed an object was. Scientists disagree about how much this shows.

items.f: Only humans can learn a language.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. Apes taught by people have learned hundreds of signs or symbols. Whether they use grammar, as language needs, is not agreed.

items.f: Only humans mind when something is unfair.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. In a 2003 test, monkeys called capuchins refused cucumber when a partner got a grape for the same job. Some scientists say they only wanted the grape they could see.

items.f: Only humans cook their food.
items.b: NOT SEEN IN OTHER APES SO FAR. No wild ape makes fire, keeps a fire going or cooks.

items.f: Only humans build on each other's inventions, until no one person could have invented the result.
items.b: NOT SEEN IN OTHER APES SO FAR. Ape tools stay simple enough for one clever ape to invent. A bicycle or a pressure cooker holds the ideas of thousands of people. A few scientists think they see small beginnings of this in apes.

items.f: Only humans write things down for others to read years later.
items.b: NOT SEEN IN OTHER APES SO FAR. No other ape leaves marks that carry a message to someone who is not there.

ask.q: What kind of evidence would move a card from 'not seen so far' to 'others do it too'?
good: Someone would have to see a wild ape do it.
It would have to be seen more than once, or filmed.
Other scientists would have to see it too.

Nobody has seen it yet, which could change
Apes will learn it soon

games.title: Learned, Place or Genes? The difference cards
games.context: This is a card game about how scientists decide that a habit is culture. Each card tells of a difference between two groups. You decide what causes the difference: something learned from others, the place, or genes.

printables.title: 12 difference cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Chimpanzees at Taï crack nuts with stone hammers. Chimpanzees at Gombe do not. Both forests have nuts and stones.
items.b: LEARNED. The place offers the same things to both groups, and both are chimpanzees. The young at Taï learn by watching for years.

items.f: One chimpanzee group never fishes for termites. Their forest has no termite mounds.
items.b: PLACE. Nobody can fish where there is nothing to fish for. This difference tells us nothing about culture.

items.f: Bonobos are slimmer than chimpanzees and have longer legs, wherever they grow up.
items.b: GENES. A bonobo raised among chimpanzees would still have a bonobo's body. Body shape is inherited.

items.f: At Mahale, two chimpanzees grooming each other clasp hands above their heads. Most other chimpanzee groups never do.
items.b: LEARNED. Nothing in the forest makes a hand clasp useful there and useless elsewhere. The young pick it up from their group.

items.f: At one pool, some chimpanzees drink with moss sponges and others with leaf sponges. The moss users all watched a moss user first.
items.b: LEARNED. They share one forest and one family tree. What differs is who watched whom.

items.f: People in Ladakh wear thick wool. People in Chennai wear thin cotton.
items.b: PLACE. Cold calls for wool and heat for cotton. How to weave each cloth is learned, but the need comes from the place.

items.f: Meenakshi's family eats rice with the right hand. Her cousin's family in Japan eats rice with chopsticks.
items.b: LEARNED. Both families have hands, and both could buy chopsticks. Each child copies the people at home.

items.f: Farhan's blood group is B. His best friend's is O. They grew up on the same street.
items.b: GENES. A blood group is inherited from parents. Nothing a child watches or learns can change it.

items.f: Orangutans in one swamp forest poke sticks into a prickly fruit to get the seeds. A nearby group with the same fruit do not.
items.b: LEARNED. The fruit and the sticks are there for both groups. Only one group has the habit to copy.

items.f: Gorillas who live high on cold mountains have longer, thicker hair than gorillas in warm lowland forest.
items.b: GENES. A mountain gorilla is born with the thicker coat. Over many generations the cold place selected for it, so place shaped the genes.

items.f: A kolam at the door in Tamil Nadu, an alpana in Bengal, a rangoli in Maharashtra.
items.b: LEARNED. Rice flour and chalk are sold everywhere. Each child learns the patterns of the people around them.

items.f: Most adults whose ancestors herded cattle can digest milk. Many adults elsewhere cannot.
items.b: BOTH LEARNED AND GENES. Keeping cattle is a learned tradition. Over thousands of years, that tradition selected for a gene that lets adults digest milk.

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, with the difference facing up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say 'learned', 'place' or 'genes', and give your reason.
Ask yourself two questions. Does the place offer the same things to both groups? Are both groups the same species or family?
Turn the card over. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
One card has two causes working together. Whoever spots it gets a bonus point.
The game ends when the pile is gone. If you play alone, count how many turns it took and try to beat that.
