ask.q: Why must scientists rule out the place before they call a habit culture?
good: A group cannot do something if the things for it are missing.
Then the difference comes from the forest and not from learning.

flow.parent: If your child guesses the label without a reason, ask the two questions on the rules list before the card is turned.
flow.context: This is the main part of the game Learned, Place or Genes? Here you decide what causes each difference between two groups.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards each player kept. 2. Sort all 12 cards by their answers. 3. Find the card with two causes.
flow.say: Sort the cards by their answers. Which pile is biggest? Which card had two causes working together?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Sort all the cards by answer. Find the card with two causes.

check.q: Two chimpanzee groups differ in a habit. What must be true before you call it culture?
options: The place could allow the habit in both groups
One group is cleverer than the other
The habit uses a tool
check.why: If the place makes the habit impossible for one group, the place explains the difference. Culture is what is left when place and genes are ruled out. If you chose 'uses a tool', remember that hand clasping is culture with no tool at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of the game Learned, Place or Genes? Here you sort the cards and see how many differences were learned.

experiments.title: The Termite Fishing Test: which stalk brings out the most seeds?
experiments.question: A chimpanzee fishes for termites with a stem. You have three stalks: one with leaves on, one stripped bare, and one stripped with the tip frayed into a brush. Which one brings the most sesame seeds out of a covered tumbler?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the three stalks will bring out the most seeds in five dips, and which the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same person fishes with all three stalks, in the same tumbler of seeds, through the same hole. Every stalk is dipped in water in the same way and held in the seeds for a count of three. Each stalk gets five dips, because one dip can be a fluke. The dips go in turn, leafy, stripped, brush, again and again, so that no stalk gets all the practice. Only one thing changes: the shape of the stalk.

materials.item: curry-leaf stalks with the leaves on, each about 15 cm long. Coriander stalks or any thin fresh twigs also work
a steel tumbler
sesame seeds (til or ellu), 3 tablespoons. Ragi also works
a sheet of paper and a rubber band, to cover the tumbler
a second tumbler, half full of water
a steel spoon and a chopping board, to fray one tip
a steel plate, to count seeds on
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each stalk: leafy, stripped and brush tip. Write the number of seeds for each of the five dips, then the total.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three fishing tools from curry-leaf stalks, as a chimpanzee makes them from stems. A covered tumbler of sesame seeds stands for a termite mound. You count which tool brings out the most seeds.

setup.art: Three curry-leaf stalks side by side on a chopping board: one with all its leaves, one stripped bare, and one stripped with its tip split into fine fibres.
setup.caption: 1. Make three tools: leafy, stripped, and stripped with a brush tip.

setup.art: A steel tumbler with paper stretched over the top and held by a rubber band, with a hole as wide as a pencil in the middle of the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the tumbler of seeds. Make a hole as wide as a pencil.

setup.art: A child dipping the tip of a stalk into a tumbler of water.
setup.caption: 3. Wet the tip. Tap off the drip.

setup.art: A child pushing the stalk down through the hole in the paper cover, counting on the fingers of the other hand.
setup.caption: 4. Push the tip to the bottom. Count to three. Pull out slowly.

setup.art: A stalk held over a steel plate, sesame seeds stuck to its wet tip, a finger brushing the seeds onto the plate.
setup.caption: 5. Brush the seeds onto the plate and count them.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seeds brought out on each dip

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three leafy stalks and the tumbler of seeds. 2. Explain the three tools they will make. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: The seeds are termites in a mound. You will fish with three stalks: leafy, stripped, and stripped with a brush tip. Which will bring out the most seeds? Which the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the stalks and the seeds. Guess which tool will catch the most. Say why.

ask.q: What do you think the leaves will do when the stalk goes into the hole?
good: They will get stuck.
They might help by holding more seeds.
They will fold back and block the hole.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children think the leafy stalk will catch most because it is biggest. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Termite Fishing Test. You guess which of three stalks will bring out the most seeds, before you try.

flow.do: 1. Leave the first stalk as it is. 2. Pull every leaf off the second stalk. 3. Pull every leaf off the third stalk. 4. Lay the last 2 cm of the third stalk on the board. Press and roll the back of the spoon on it ten times. 5. Split the squashed end into thin fibres with a fingernail.
flow.say: Leave one stalk leafy. Strip the leaves off the other two. Now squash the tip of the third and split it into a little brush.
flow.kid: Keep one stalk leafy. Strip the other two. Squash one tip and split it into a brush.
flow.parent: A fresh green stalk frays best. If the tip will not split, tie five short pieces of thread round it, with 2 cm of each hanging free. Chimpanzees fray a stem by pulling it through their teeth. Your child may try that too, since curry-leaf stalks are safe to chew.
flow.context: In this step of the Termite Fishing Test you make the three tools: a leafy stalk, a stripped stalk and a stalk with a brush tip.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 tablespoons of sesame seeds in the dry steel tumbler. 2. Stretch the paper over the top and hold it with the rubber band. 3. Push a pencil through the middle of the paper to make one hole. 4. Draw the results table.
flow.say: This is the termite mound. The hole is the only way in, and you cannot see inside. A chimpanzee cannot see inside a mound either.
flow.kid: Put the seeds in the tumbler. Cover it with paper. Make one pencil hole. Draw your table.
flow.parent: Keep the hole no wider than a pencil. A real termite tunnel is narrow, and the narrow hole is what makes the leaves a problem.
flow.context: In this step of the Termite Fishing Test you make the covered tumbler of seeds that stands for a termite mound.

flow.do: 1. Dip the bottom 3 cm of the leafy stalk in water and tap off the drip. 2. Push it through the hole to the bottom, without tearing the paper. 3. Count to three and pull it out slowly. 4. Brush the seeds onto the plate, count them and write the number. 5. Do the same with the stripped stalk, then the brush tip. 6. Repeat until each stalk has had five dips.
flow.say: Wet the tip, push it in, count to three, and pull out slowly. Count the seeds. Now the next stalk. We go round five times.
flow.kid: Wet the tip. Push it in and count to three. Pull out slowly. Count the seeds.
flow.parent: If the leafy stalk will not go through, that dip scores 0. Do not force it. Wet the tip before every dip, because the seeds stick to the water. If almost no seeds stick to any stalk, the tips are too dry. Clear the plate after each count.

check.q: In the Termite Fishing Test, why do you fish in turn and not five times with one stalk first?
options: So no stalk gets all your practice
So the seeds stay dry
So the game lasts longer
check.why: You get better at fishing as you go. If one stalk had all the late dips, it would score higher because of your practice, and not because of its shape. If you chose 'seeds stay dry', notice that every stalk is wet in the same way.

flow.context: In this step of the Termite Fishing Test you fish for seeds five times with each of the three stalks, and count the seeds each time.

flow.do: 1. Add up the five dips for each stalk. 2. Write the three totals. 3. Draw a bar for each total.
flow.say: Add up each row. Now draw three bars, one for each stalk. Which bar is tallest?
flow.kid: Add up each row. Draw a bar for each stalk. Which is tallest?
flow.parent: A bar chart suits these results, because the three stalks are separate things to compare.
flow.context: In this step of the Termite Fishing Test you add up the seeds for each stalk and draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table and the chart together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. What did you do to the stalk to make it work better?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did stripping the leaves help?
good: The leaves caught on the hole.
A bare stalk could reach the seeds.

ask.q: Why might a brush tip hold more seeds than a plain tip?
good: It has more wet surface for seeds to stick to.
Seeds get caught between the fibres.

flow.parent: In most homes the brush tip brings out the most seeds and the leafy stalk the fewest. Write down what you really found. If the brush did not win, look at its tip. Fibres that have stuck together into one point act like a plain tip. The reason: a stalk only works if it fits the hole, and a frayed tip has more surface. Real termites bite on to anything pushed into their nest, and a brush gives them more to bite. In a real test in the Republic of Congo in 2009, brush tips brought out about 5 termites each try. Plain stems brought out about 1 termite in every 4 tries. Your child changed a stalk twice to fit a job. That is tool making, and chimpanzees do both of those steps.
flow.think: You knew what the tool was for before you made it. What must a chimpanzee know before stripping a stem?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Termite Fishing Test. You say what your counts show about the three stalks.

experiments.title: The Copycat Test: do people copy a step that does nothing?
experiments.question: You show someone how to get a sweet out of a clear box. Before you open the lid, you tap the lid three times and turn the box round. Anyone can see these steps do nothing. Will people copy them?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many of the people you test will tap the lid, and how many will turn the box? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every person sees the same four steps, done in the same order at the same speed. You say the same words to each person and never say 'copy me'. Each person is tested alone, so nobody watches anyone else's turn. The box, the spoon and the sweet are the same each time. Only the person changes.
results_table: What they said when asked why

materials.item: a clear plastic box or jar with a lid that opens easily
small sweets, raisins or groundnuts, one for each person
a steel spoon
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each person. Write their age, whether they tapped the lid, whether they turned the box, and what they said when you asked why.
experiments.context: In this experiment you are the scientist and your family and friends are the ones being tested. You find out whether people copy steps that clearly do nothing. You need at least three people who have not read this page.

setup.art: A clear plastic box with a lid on a table, a wrapped sweet visible inside, and a steel spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put one sweet in the clear box. Close the lid.

setup.art: A child tapping the lid of the box with a spoon while a grandmother watches from across the table.
setup.caption: 2. Tap the lid three times. Turn the box round once.

setup.art: The child lifting the lid and taking out the sweet.
setup.caption: 3. Open the lid and take the sweet.

setup.art: The grandmother alone with the box and spoon, the child watching with a notebook held behind her back.
setup.caption: 4. Put in a new sweet. Say: 'Your turn to get the sweet.' Watch what they do.

flow.do: 1. Read the question with your child. 2. Make a list of at least three people to test. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each person, and write them down.
flow.say: The box is clear, so anyone can see that tapping does nothing. Who on your list will tap anyway? Who will go straight for the lid? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: List three people to test. Guess who will tap the lid. Say why.

ask.q: Do you think grown-ups or small children will copy more? Why?
good: Small children, because they copy everything.
Grown-ups, because they want to do it properly.
Nobody, because they can see it is useless.

flow.parent: You can be tested only if you have not read this page. If you have, help with the list. Grandparents, neighbours, cousins and friends all count.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Copycat Test. You choose whom to test and guess who will copy the useless steps.

flow.do: 1. Your child practises the four steps until they are smooth. Tap the lid three times with the spoon. Turn the box round once on the table. Open the lid. Take the sweet. 2. They practise the words too.
flow.say: Practise until you do it the same way every time. Say only this: 'Watch how I get the sweet.' Afterwards say: 'Your turn to get the sweet.'
flow.kid: Practise: tap three times, turn the box, open, take the sweet. Learn your two sentences.
flow.parent: The words matter. 'Copy me' would tell people what to do. 'Your turn to get the sweet' names only the goal.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you practise showing the four steps in exactly the same way each time.

flow.do: 1. Bring in the first person alone. 2. Your child shows the four steps once. 3. They put in a new sweet, close the lid and hand over the spoon. 4. They watch without speaking, and write what the person did after the person leaves. 5. Do the same with each person.
flow.say: Show the steps once. Then give them the spoon and say your sentence. Do not help, and do not smile at the tapping.
flow.kid: Show each person the steps once. Give them the spoon. Watch quietly. Write what they did.
flow.parent: Keep the others out of the room, so nobody sees a turn before their own. Each person keeps the sweet they get.

check.q: In the Copycat Test, why is each person tested alone?
options: So they copy only what you showed
So they do not eat all the sweets
So they feel shy
check.why: If people watch each other, they may copy the person before them. Then you cannot tell what your own showing did. If you chose 'sweets', remember that each person gets only one.

flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you show the steps to each person alone and write down what they copy.

flow.do: 1. Count how many people tapped the lid and how many turned the box. 2. Go back to each person and ask why they did, or did not. 3. Write their answers in the last column.
flow.say: Count the taps and the turns. Now go and ask each person one thing. Why did you tap, or why did you not?
flow.kid: Count who tapped and who turned. Ask each person why. Write what they say.
flow.parent: The answers are often the best part. People say 'because you did' or 'I thought it was part of it'. Some cannot say why at all.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you count your results and ask each person why they copied or did not.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it might have happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why you think people did that. When could copying a step you do not understand be useful?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why people might copy.

ask.q: When is it useful to copy a step you do not understand?
good: When the job is too complicated to see why each step matters.
In cooking, or tying a sari, or a science method.
When the person showing you knows more than you.

flow.parent: With three or four people, your result may go either way. Write down what you really found. In 2005 Victoria Horner and Andrew Whiten ran a test like this with a puzzle box. Young chimpanzees who could see through the box left out the useless step. Children of three and four copied every step, even with the clear box. Some scientists think this habit is what lets human skills build up. Many human skills are too complicated for a learner to see why each step matters. Think of soaking, grinding and fermenting for idli batter. Copying exactly keeps the steps that work, even when nobody remembers why. This is an idea and not a settled fact. The chimpanzees in the test were being sensible.
flow.think: The chimpanzees skipped the useless step and the children did not. Who was being clever?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Copycat Test. You say what your results show about how people copy.

activities.title: The Only-Humans List: what can only humans do?
activities.context: This activity comes first in the lesson. You write your own list of things that you think only humans can do. You keep the list, and check it against the evidence later.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
an envelope, or a book to keep the list in

activities.record: A list of six sentences that begin 'Only humans can', each with a reason and a mark for 'sure' or 'not sure'.

setup.art: A sheet of paper headed 'Only humans can...' with six numbered lines, a child writing on the second line.
setup.caption: 1. Write six things you think only humans can do.

setup.art: The same sheet with a tick or a question mark beside each line.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each one: sure, or not sure.

setup.art: A child sliding the folded list into an envelope.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the list. You will check it later.

flow.do: 1. Give your child paper and a pencil. 2. They write 'Only humans can' six times down the page. 3. They finish each sentence, and say a reason for each one.
flow.say: Think of all the other animals. What can only humans do? Write six things. Tell me your reason for each.
flow.kid: Write 'Only humans can' six times. Finish each sentence. Say your reason for each.
flow.parent: Write your own list too, on another sheet, and do not show it yet. Do not correct anything. Common answers are talk, make tools, cook, use money, feel sad, read and build houses.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Only-Humans List. You write six things you think only humans can do.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts a tick beside each sentence they are sure of, and a question mark beside the others. 2. They choose the one they are surest of and draw a ring round it. 3. Compare your two lists.
flow.say: Tick the ones you are sure about. Put a question mark by the rest. Which one are you surest of? How could someone check it?
flow.kid: Tick the ones you are sure of. Ring the one you are surest of.

ask.q: How could someone find out whether another animal does this?
good: Watch the animals for a long time.
Go where they live.
Set them a puzzle and see.

flow.context: In this step of The Only-Humans List you mark how sure you are of each sentence.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that scientists in 1960 had a list like this. 2. Tell them the first thing on it was 'make tools'. 3. Put both lists in the envelope for later.
flow.say: In 1960, scientists had a list like yours. At the top was 'make tools'. Next, you will make a tool the way a chimpanzee does. Keep your list safe.
flow.kid: Scientists once had a list like yours. 'Make tools' was at the top. Keep your list safe.
flow.parent: Bring the lists out again after the game Only Humans?, or at the end of the unit. Ask what your child would cross out, and what they would keep.
flow.think: If something is on your list today, does that mean no other animal does it? Or that nobody has seen it yet?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Only-Humans List. You hear what was at the top of the scientists' list in 1960.

activities.title: The Hundred Square: what does 'almost 99 per cent the same' mean?
activities.context: People say human DNA and chimpanzee DNA are almost 99 per cent the same. In this activity you draw that number on a square of 100 boxes. Then you find out why the number changes with how you count.

materials.item: a page from a squared maths notebook
a red pencil and a blue pencil
a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: A square of 100 boxes with 1 red box and 3 blue boxes, and your two sums written under it.

setup.art: A square of 10 by 10 boxes outlined on squared paper.
setup.caption: 1. Outline a square of 100 boxes.

setup.art: The same square with one box coloured red.
setup.caption: 2. Colour 1 box red for single letters that differ.

setup.art: The same square with one red box and three blue boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Colour 3 boxes blue for stretches that are added or missing.

flow.do: 1. Your child outlines a square of 10 boxes by 10 boxes. 2. Tell them each box stands for one DNA letter in every hundred. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: These 100 boxes stand for your DNA. How many boxes do you think are different in a chimpanzee? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Outline 100 boxes. Guess how many are different in a chimpanzee. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children guess 20 or 30, because a chimpanzee looks so different from a person. Write the guess beside the square.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Hundred Square. You guess how much of a chimpanzee's DNA differs from yours.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours 1 box red. This is for single letters that differ. 2. They colour 3 boxes blue. These are for stretches that one species has and the other lacks. 3. They count the boxes left white.
flow.say: Colour one box red. Those are letters that differ when the two are lined up. Now three blue, for stretches that are added or missing. How many are left white?
flow.kid: Colour 1 box red. Colour 3 boxes blue. Count the white boxes.
flow.parent: The exact figure for single letters is about 1.2 in 100, so the red box should really be a little bigger than one box. With the blue boxes, 96 stay white. Counting only red gives 'almost 99 per cent'. Counting red and blue gives '96 per cent'. Both are honest. They count different things.

check.q: One book says humans and chimpanzees are 99 per cent alike. Another says 96. What is the likeliest reason?
options: They counted different kinds of difference
One book made a mistake
Chimpanzees changed between the books
check.why: The first counts only single letters that differ. The second also counts stretches that are added or missing. If you chose 'a mistake', remember that both numbers come from the same 2005 study.

flow.context: In this step of The Hundred Square you colour the boxes that differ between human and chimpanzee DNA.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that one set of human DNA has about 3,000 million letters. 2. They work out how many letters one box stands for. 3. They work out how many letters 1.2 boxes stand for. 4. Tell them two humans differ by about one tenth of a box.
flow.say: Your DNA has about 3,000 million letters. So how many letters is one box? How many is 1.2 boxes? Is that a small number?
flow.kid: Your DNA has 3,000 million letters. How many is one box? How many is 1.2 boxes?

ask.q: The red box looks tiny. Is the difference between you and a chimpanzee small or large?
good: Small as a share, but 36 million letters is a lot.
It depends whether you look at the share or the count.

flow.parent: 3,000 million ÷ 100 = 30 million letters for one box. 30 million × 1.2 = 36 million letters. The 2005 study counted about 35 million. Two humans differ at about 1 letter in 1,000, which is one tenth of a box, or about 3 million letters.
flow.think: Would you say 'only 1 in 100' or 'as many as 36 million'? Both are true. Why might someone choose one or the other?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Hundred Square. You work out how many DNA letters the red box stands for.

activities.title: The Joined Chromosome: a guess that could have failed
activities.context: Humans have 46 chromosomes and the other great apes have 48. In this activity you join two paper chromosomes into one. You predict what marks a join would leave, and then compare with what scientists found.

materials.item: strips of paper about 2 cm wide: one 10 cm long and one 8 cm long
a red pencil and a black pencil
sticky tape

activities.record: A drawing of your joined strip, with the marks labelled, and one sentence saying what scientists found.

setup.art: Two paper strips, one longer than the other, each with both ends coloured red and a black dot near the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Make two chromosomes. Colour the ends red. Put a black dot near the middle of each.

setup.art: The two strips taped end to end into one long strip, with two red patches meeting in the middle and two black dots.
setup.caption: 2. Tape them end to end. Look at the middle.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours 1 cm at both ends of each strip red. 2. They draw a black dot near the middle of each strip. 3. Explain what the marks stand for.
flow.say: Each strip is a chromosome. Every chromosome has special end letters, here in red. Each has one pinched-in place, the black dot, used when a cell divides.
flow.kid: Colour both ends of each strip red. Draw one black dot on each.
flow.parent: The real name for the ends is telomeres and for the pinched-in place is the centromere. Use the words if your child likes them.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Joined Chromosome. You make two paper chromosomes with marked ends and middles.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that apes have 48 chromosomes and humans 46, which is one pair fewer. 2. Ask what a chromosome made from two joined ones would look like. 3. They draw their guess. 4. Then they tape the strips end to end.
flow.say: Other great apes have one pair of chromosomes more than we do. Suppose two joined into one on our line. What marks would the join leave? Draw your guess, then tape the strips.
flow.kid: Suppose two chromosomes joined into one. Draw what it would look like. Then tape your strips.

ask.q: Look at your taped strip. What is odd about it, compared with a normal chromosome?
good: It has red end marks in the middle.
It has two black dots, not one.

flow.context: In this step of The Joined Chromosome you predict what marks a join would leave, and then tape the two strips together.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child what scientists found in human chromosome 2. 2. They label their strip. 3. They write one sentence about what was found.
flow.say: In 1991, scientists found end letters in the middle of our chromosome 2. In 1992, others found the faded remains of a second pinched-in place. Does that match your strip?
flow.kid: Scientists found end letters in the middle of chromosome 2. Does your strip match?
flow.parent: The DNA on each side of the join matches a separate chimpanzee chromosome. The second pinched-in place no longer works, which is why the chromosome behaves normally.

check.q: Why is finding end letters in the middle of chromosome 2 strong evidence?
options: The join idea predicted it before anyone looked
End letters are very rare
Chromosome 2 is the biggest chromosome
check.why: The idea said what should be there. Scientists looked, and it was there. If it had not been, the idea would have been in trouble. If you chose 'the biggest', note that chromosome 1 is bigger.

flow.think: A good guess in science is one that could turn out wrong. Why is that better than a guess that fits anything?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Joined Chromosome. You compare your taped strip with what scientists found in human chromosome 2.

activities.title: One Glance: the number memory test a chimpanzee took
activities.context: In 2007 a young chimpanzee named Ayumu did a memory test better than university students. In this activity you take a paper form of that test, and so does a grown-up.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, all the same size
a thick pen and a pencil

activities.record: A score for each sheet: how many numbers you put in the right place, for 5 numbers, 7 numbers and 9 numbers.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with the numbers 1 to 5 written large in scattered places.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up writes 1 to 5 in scattered places on a sheet.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the sheet up towards a child for a moment.
setup.caption: 2. Look for one count. Then the sheet goes face down.

setup.art: A child writing numbers on a blank sheet from memory, the first sheet lying face down beside it.
setup.caption: 3. On a blank sheet, write each number where it was.

flow.do: 1. Out of your child's sight, write the numbers 1 to 5 on a sheet, large and scattered. 2. Make three sheets like this, each with different places. 3. Make two sheets with 1 to 7 and one with 1 to 9. 4. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: You will see some numbers for one second. Then you write each one where it was. How many numbers do you think you can hold? Who will do better, you or me? Why?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes six number sheets. Guess how many numbers you can hold. Say why.
flow.parent: Spread the numbers out, with none in a neat row. Keep the sheets face down in a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Glance. A grown-up makes the number sheets and you guess how you will do.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the first sheet. Say 'Look', count 'one', and turn it face down. 2. Your child writes each number on a blank sheet, where they think it was. 3. Lay the two sheets side by side. Count the numbers within two finger-widths of the right place. 4. Do all six sheets.
flow.say: Look. One. Now write each number where it was. Let's put the sheets side by side and count the ones you got.
flow.kid: Look for one count. Write each number where it was. Count how many you got.
flow.parent: Expect few mistakes with 5 numbers and many more with 7 or 9. Scores often rise from the first sheet to the third. That is practice at work.
flow.context: In this step of One Glance you see each sheet for one count and write the numbers from memory.

flow.do: 1. Swap places. Your child makes three new sheets and tests you. 2. Compare your scores. 3. Tell your child about Ayumu.
flow.say: Now test me. Ayumu saw five numbers for a fifth of a second, much less than your one count. He was right about 8 times in 10. Why might a chimpanzee be so good at this?
flow.kid: Make three sheets and test a grown-up. Compare scores. Why might a chimpanzee be good at this?

ask.q: Your scores went up with practice. What does that tell you about comparing Ayumu with the students?
good: Ayumu had practised a lot and the students had not.
It was not a fair test unless both practised.

flow.parent: Ayumu had practised the task for a long time. In 2009 other scientists gave two people a lot of practice, and they matched him. So the test shows that a chimpanzee's memory for a glance is very good, and that practice matters. Some scientists think this memory helps in a forest, where a chimpanzee must take in a whole scene at once.

check.q: Ayumu had practised for years and the students had not. What does that mean for the comparison?
options: It was not a fully fair test
Chimpanzees are cleverer than people
Practice makes no difference
check.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here two things differed: the species and the amount of practice. If you chose 'cleverer', remember that one task cannot rank whole minds.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Glance. You test a grown-up and hear how the chimpanzee Ayumu did.

activities.title: Hammer and Anvil: crack ten groundnuts whole
activities.context: Chimpanzees in the Taï forest crack hard nuts with a stone hammer on a flat stone or root. A young chimpanzee takes years to get good at it. In this activity you try it with groundnuts and feel why.

materials.item: groundnuts in their shells
a smooth stone that fits your hand, or a small pestle or rolling pin
a wooden chopping board
a steel plate

activities.safety: A grown-up stays close. Keep the fingers of the other hand flat on the board, away from the nut. Do not use this for children who are allergic to groundnuts.
activities.record: For each round of 10 nuts, write how many shells you opened with one hit while keeping both nuts inside whole.

setup.art: A wooden chopping board on the floor with one groundnut in the shell on it, and a smooth stone beside it.
setup.caption: 1. The board is your anvil. The stone is your hammer.

setup.art: A child's hand bringing the stone down on the groundnut, the other hand flat on the board well away from the nut.
setup.caption: 2. One hit. Keep your other hand away.

setup.art: A steel plate with whole groundnuts on one side and crushed pieces on the other.
setup.caption: 3. Whole nuts on one side, crushed on the other. Count.

flow.do: 1. Put the board on the floor. 2. Show the rule: one hit for each nut. The shell must open and both nuts inside must stay whole. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: One hit for each nut. Too soft and the shell stays shut. Too hard and the nut is crushed. How many out of ten will you get whole? Why?
flow.kid: One hit for each nut. Open the shell but keep the nuts whole. Guess your score out of ten.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hammer and Anvil. You learn the rule and guess how many groundnuts you can crack whole.

flow.do: 1. Your child cracks 10 groundnuts, one hit each. 2. They put whole nuts on one side of the plate and crushed ones on the other. 3. They count and write the score. 4. They do a second round of 10 and write that score.
flow.say: Ten nuts, one hit each. Count the whole ones. Now ten more. Did you change anything the second time?
flow.kid: Crack 10 nuts with one hit each. Count the whole ones. Then do 10 more.

ask.q: What did you change between the first round and the second?
good: I hit more gently.
I turned the nut on its side.
I held the stone lower down.

flow.parent: Most children score higher in the second round. If the score is 10 in round one, your child uses the other hand in round two.
flow.context: In this step of Hammer and Anvil you crack two rounds of ten groundnuts and count how many stay whole.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two scores. 2. Tell your child how long a young chimpanzee takes to learn. 3. Eat the groundnuts.
flow.say: You got better in ten tries. The nuts at Taï are far harder than these, and the hammers are heavy stones or wooden clubs. Why might learning take a chimpanzee years?
flow.kid: Compare your two scores. Why might a young chimpanzee need years to learn this?
flow.parent: Three things must be right at once: where the nut sits, which stone is chosen, and how hard the hit is. A young chimpanzee watches the mother, plays with stones and nuts, and often uses the mother's own hammer. Stones dug up at Taï show that chimpanzees there were cracking nuts 4,300 years ago.
flow.think: You were told the rule in words. A young chimpanzee gets no words. What would you have to work out by watching alone?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hammer and Anvil. You compare your two rounds and think about how a young chimpanzee learns.

activities.title: Talking Without Words: can your family read your gestures?
activities.context: Wild chimpanzees ask each other for things with dozens of gestures. In this activity you give eight messages with your hands and body alone, and count how many your family can read.

materials.item: small slips of paper
a bowl
a pencil

activities.record: A score out of 8: how many messages were guessed right on the first try.

setup.art: Eight folded paper slips in a steel bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Write one message on each slip. Fold them into a bowl.

setup.art: A child holding out an open hand, palm up, towards a grown-up who is eating, lips pressed shut.
setup.caption: 2. Give the message with hands and body only. No sounds.

setup.art: A grown-up pointing to one of four choices written on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 3. The others guess the message.

flow.do: 1. Write these eight messages on slips: Give me some of that. Come here. Groom me here. Stop that. Let's play. Move away. Climb on my back. Follow me. 2. Fold the slips into the bowl. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: You will give each message with no words and no sounds. How many out of eight will we guess the first time? Why?
flow.kid: Write the eight messages on slips. Guess how many your family will read.
flow.context: This is the first step of Talking Without Words. You make eight message slips and guess how many will be understood.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a slip and reads it silently. 2. They give the message with hands, face and body only. 3. The others get one guess. 4. Mark a tick for each right first guess. 5. Go through all eight.
flow.say: Read the slip to yourself. Now tell us with your body only. We get one guess.
flow.kid: Take a slip. Give the message with no words or sounds. The others guess once.
flow.parent: Guess honestly, and say your guess as a whole message, such as 'you want me to follow you'.
flow.context: In this step of Talking Without Words you give eight messages by gesture and count the right guesses.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks. 2. Tell your child that all eight messages are real chimpanzee messages. 3. Show two real chimpanzee gestures: an open hand held out, and a long loud scratch on your own arm.
flow.say: All eight are things wild chimpanzees ask each other. An open hand means 'give me some'. A big loud scratch on the arm means 'groom me here'. Did you use either?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Chimpanzees send all eight messages. Did you use an open hand?

ask.q: Why might people understand chimpanzee gestures without being taught?
good: We may have had the same gestures from our common ancestors.
Our bodies are alike, so the same movements make sense.
Babies use some of them before they talk.

flow.parent: In 2023, 5,656 people watched films of chimpanzee and bonobo gestures online. They picked the right meaning out of four more than half the time. Guessing would give 1 in 4. Scientists do not know whether we inherit this understanding or work it out each time.

check.q: What makes a movement a gesture, and not only a movement?
options: It is made on purpose to tell another something
It is made with the hands
It is loud
check.why: A gesture is aimed at someone. The gesturer watches for an answer and tries again if none comes. If you chose 'hands', remember that a whole body can gesture, such as turning your back to be groomed.

flow.context: This is the last step of Talking Without Words. You count the messages your family read and compare with real chimpanzee gestures.

projects.title: A Tradition Map: is it learned, the place or genes?
projects.context: In 1999 scientists made a table of chimpanzee habits and groups, to find which habits were culture. In this three-day project you make the same kind of table for four human households, and trace who learned each habit from whom.

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
a phone, with a grown-up, to call relatives or friends
a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Choose eight habits that might differ between households. Draw the table and fill in your own household's column.
Ask three other households about the same eight habits. Fill in their columns with 'always', 'sometimes' or 'never'.
For each habit that differs, decide whether the cause is learned, the place or genes. Draw a map of who learned from whom, and tell your family what you found.

projects.record: A table with eight rows of habits and four columns of households. A map with arrows showing who learned one habit from whom.

setup.art: A notebook table with habits listed down the side, such as 'drinks water without lips touching the tumbler', and four household names across the top.
setup.caption: 1. List eight habits. Fill in your own household.

setup.art: A child on a phone call, writing 'always', 'sometimes' or 'never' into the table.
setup.caption: 2. Ask three other households the same questions.

setup.art: A large sheet with names joined by arrows, labelled 'Paati showed Amma', 'Amma showed me'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw who learned one habit from whom.

flow.do: 1. Help your child choose eight habits from the list in the note below, or their own. 2. They rule a table with eight rows and four columns. 3. They fill in the column for your own household with 'always', 'sometimes' or 'never'.
flow.say: Chimpanzee scientists listed habits down one side and groups across the top. Let's do it for people. Which eight habits might differ from one home to the next?
flow.kid: Choose eight habits. Rule a table. Fill in your own home with always, sometimes or never.
flow.parent: Good habits to ask about: drinking water without the lips touching the tumbler. Eating rice with the hand. Peeling a banana from the stalk end. Counting on finger joints with the thumb. Drawing a kolam or rangoli at the door. Taking off chappals at the door. Sleeping on a mat on the floor. What people say when someone sneezes.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Tradition Map. Here you choose eight habits and record what your own household does.

flow.do: 1. Your child calls or visits three other households, such as grandparents, a cousin's family and a friend's family. 2. They ask about each of the eight habits. 3. They write 'always', 'sometimes' or 'never' in each box.
flow.say: Ask each family the same eight questions, in the same words. Write always, sometimes or never. Try a family from another town or state if you can.
flow.kid: Ask three other homes the same eight questions. Write always, sometimes or never.
flow.parent: Households from different regions give the most interesting table. Asking in the same words each time keeps the comparison fair.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Tradition Map. Here you ask three other households about the same eight habits.

flow.do: 1. Your child rings every row where the households differ. 2. For each ringed row they decide: learned, the place, or genes, with a reason. 3. They choose one learned habit and ask who taught whom, back as far as anyone knows. 4. They draw this as a map with arrows and present it.
flow.say: Ring the rows that differ. For each one, could the place explain it? Could genes? If not, it is learned. Pick one and find out who learned it from whom.
flow.kid: Ring the rows that differ. Decide the cause of each. Draw who learned one habit from whom.

ask.q: How far back could you trace one habit? What happens to the map before that?
good: Only to my great-grandmother.
Nobody remembers who started it.
It goes back further than anyone can say.

flow.parent: Most rows will be 'learned'. A few may be 'the place', such as sleeping on a mat in a hot town. Almost none will be 'genes'. That is the point: most of what differs between human homes is culture. The map of who taught whom is the same kind of record Catherine Hobaiter kept for moss sponges.
flow.context: This is day 3 of A Tradition Map. Here you decide what causes each difference and trace who learned one habit from whom.

challenges.title: The Nut in the Bottle: get it out without tipping
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that scientists gave to orangutans, chimpanzees and children. A groundnut lies at the bottom of a tall, narrow bottle that must stay upright. Try it yourself before you read the solutions below.
challenges.problem: A groundnut in the shell is at the bottom of an empty 500 millilitre bottle. Get the groundnut out. The bottle must stay standing on the tray the whole time.
constraints: The bottle stays upright on the tray. No tipping, lifting, squeezing or cutting.
You may use anything that is on the table.
You have 8 minutes for your first try.
Nobody may tell you the answer during those 8 minutes.
materials: an empty 500 millilitre plastic bottle with a narrow neck
a groundnut in the shell, small enough to drop through the neck
a steel tray or thali to stand the bottle on
a jug holding at least 600 millilitres of water, and a tumbler
two bamboo skewers or broom sticks, a piece of string, a spoon and sticky tape
general: Pour water into the bottle. A groundnut in the shell floats, so it rises with the water until you can pick it out at the neck.
This is what orangutans did in 2007. All five carried water from a drinker in their mouths and spat it into the tube, on their first try.
creative: Roll a loop of sticky tape, sticky side out, round the end of a skewer. Press it on the groundnut and lift.
Use two skewers as long chopsticks.
Make a noose of string at the end of a skewer and loop it round the middle of the shell.
challenges.your_turn: Now set a puzzle for a grown-up. Change one thing so that water no longer works, such as using a raisin, which sinks. Which of your other solutions still works? Design one more.

setup.art: An empty plastic bottle standing on a steel thali, a groundnut in the shell lying at the bottom of the bottle.
setup.caption: 1. Drop the groundnut into the bottle. Stand the bottle on the tray.

setup.art: A table with the bottle on its tray, and beside it a jug of water, a tumbler, two skewers, string, a spoon and tape.
setup.caption: 2. Put all the other things on the table. Say nothing about them.

setup.art: A child looking closely at the bottle with her chin in her hand, a timer running on a phone.
setup.caption: 3. Eight minutes. The bottle must stay upright.

flow.do: 1. Set out the bottle on the tray, with the groundnut inside. 2. Put the jug, tumbler, skewers, string, spoon and tape on the table. 3. Read out the problem and the rules. 4. Start a timer for 8 minutes.
flow.say: The groundnut must come out. The bottle must stay standing. You may use anything on the table. You have eight minutes.
flow.kid: Get the groundnut out. Keep the bottle standing. Use anything on the table.
flow.parent: Do not point at the jug or look at it. In the study, the children had just used the water to water plants, and most still did not think of it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Nut in the Bottle. Here the puzzle is set out and you hear the rules.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries for up to 8 minutes. 2. Stay quiet. At 4 minutes, say only the sentence below. 3. Write down each thing they try.
flow.say: You can do it. Use anything on the table.
flow.kid: Try for 8 minutes. Write down or say each thing you try.
flow.parent: Each failed try is useful. If they reach the answer early, go on to the next step. If the 8 minutes run out, that is what happened to most children in the study too.
flow.context: In this step of The Nut in the Bottle you try to get the groundnut out for up to 8 minutes.

flow.do: 1. If the nut is still in the bottle, give one hint: 'What does a groundnut do in water?' 2. Let them finish. 3. Tell them how orangutans and children did on this puzzle.
flow.say: Five orangutans were given this puzzle. All five solved it on the first try, by spitting in mouthfuls of water. About 6 in 10 eight-year-olds solved it. Why is it hard?
flow.kid: Orangutans solved this by spitting in water. Many children did not solve it. Why is it hard?

ask.q: Why is it hard to think of water as a tool?
good: Water is for drinking, so I did not see it as a tool.
A tool is usually something solid you hold.
I was only looking at the sticks.

flow.parent: In the 2011 study, about 1 in 12 four-year-olds, 4 in 10 six-year-olds and 6 in 10 eight-year-olds solved it. Among chimpanzees, about 1 in 5 did at one sanctuary. Nobody is sure why orangutans did so well.

check.q: An orangutan spits water into a tube so that a nut floats up. What does this show?
options: Using a thing in a new way to solve a problem
Orangutans like water more than nuts
The orangutan was trained to spit
check.why: Water is normally for drinking. Using it to lift something is a new use, thought of on the spot. If you chose 'trained', note that the orangutans had never seen the puzzle before.

flow.context: In this step of The Nut in the Bottle you finish the puzzle and hear how orangutans and children did on it.

flow.do: 1. Empty the bottle and dry the groundnut. 2. Your child finds a second way that uses no water. 3. Then they set a new puzzle for you.
flow.say: Now get it out without water. Then change one thing and set the puzzle for me.
flow.kid: Find a second way with no water. Then set a puzzle for a grown-up.
flow.parent: The tape loop on a skewer is the quickest dry way. If your child swaps the groundnut for a raisin, water stops working and you will need a dry way too.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Nut in the Bottle. Here you find a second solution and set a new puzzle for a grown-up.

items.p: Which of these Indian primates is an ape?
items.why: A hoolock gibbon has no tail and swings by the arms, as apes do. Macaques and langurs are monkeys with tails. A loris is a small night primate. Choosing a monkey usually means using 'ape' for any primate.

items.p: Humans, chimpanzees and bonobos share a common ____ who lived about 6 to 8 million years ago.
items.why: A common ancestor is a being from long ago from whom two kinds today both descend.

items.p: True or false: humans evolved from chimpanzees.
items.why: False. Humans and chimpanzees both descend from ancestors who were neither. Since the split, both lines have changed for the same length of time.

items.p: Match each chimpanzee tool to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool is shaped for one job. A strong answer can say what would go wrong with the wrong tool.

items.p: Sort these primates into great apes, small apes and monkeys.
items.a: see items
items.why: Great apes are the large apes, including humans. Gibbons are small apes. Macaques and langurs have tails and are monkeys.

items.p: In a fishing test, a leafy stalk brought almost no seeds through a narrow hole. Explain why.
items.a: The leaves caught on the edge of the narrow hole, so the stalk could not reach the seeds. Stripping the leaves lets the stalk pass through.
items.why: A strong answer links the shape of the tool to the shape of the hole. A real termite tunnel is narrow too.

items.p: Put in order the steps a chimpanzee takes to fish with a brush-tipped stem.
a: Fray the tip with the teeth
Push the stem into the nest
Pull it out and eat the termites
items.why: The tool is made before it is used. Stripping and fraying both change the stem to fit the job.
items: Fray the tip with the teeth
Pull it out and eat the termites
Push the stem into the nest

items.p: A chimpanzee strips a twig before fishing. Why do scientists call this making a tool?
opts: The twig was changed to fit a job
The twig lay near a mound
items.why: Making a tool means changing an object so that it does a job better. Choosing 'held the twig' describes using a thing, which is less than making one.

items.p: Three of these are great apes. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A gibbon is an ape, but a small ape. Gorillas, orangutans, bonobos, chimpanzees and humans are the great apes.

items.p: Draw a family tree for gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans.
items.a: A tree where gibbons branch off first, then orangutans, then gorillas. The last fork leads to humans on one side and to chimpanzees and bonobos on the other.
items.why: A strong drawing puts humans inside the tree and not at the top. Chimpanzees and bonobos share the fork nearest to humans.
items.art: A blank tree trunk with six empty branch tips to label.

items.p: True or false: a chimpanzee is more closely related to a human than to a gorilla.
items.why: True. The gorilla line split off first. The human line and the chimpanzee line shared ancestors for longer.

items.p: When do scientists say that a group of animals has culture?
opts: Its learned habits differ from other groups'
items.why: Culture is a set of traditions learned from others, which differs from group to group. Choosing 'stone tools' mixes up one kind of tradition with the whole idea.

items.p: Two scientists argue about how to record wild chimpanzees.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as: names help you follow one life for decades. It also says what the other has right: we must be careful not to imagine feelings that are not there.
items.why: Most ape scientists now use names. The first scientist's worry about imagining too much is still a fair one.

views.says: Give each animal a number. Names make you imagine human feelings.
Give each a name. Each has a character you must follow for years.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with more? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other has right.

items.p: Label a drawing of termite fishing: termite mound, tunnel, stripped stem, brush tip, termites.
items.why: The stem must be bare to fit the tunnel. The brush tip gives the termites more to hold.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of a termite mound with a stem pushed down a tunnel, with blank label lines.

items.p: For months the Gombe chimpanzees ran from Jane Goodall. What did she do, and why did it work?
items.a: She kept coming back to the same place every day and stayed quiet. Over months the chimpanzees learned that she was harmless and let her stay near.
items.why: Wild animals behave normally only when they no longer fear the watcher. That takes patience, which is why field studies take years.

items.p: Lined up letter by letter, about how many DNA letters in 100 differ between you and a chimpanzee?
items.why: About 1.2 letters in every 100 differ. Choosing a large number usually comes from how different our bodies look. Small DNA changes can have large effects.

items.p: True or false: a human cell has 46 chromosomes and a chimpanzee cell has 48.
items.why: True. Two chromosomes joined end to end on the human line, so we have one pair fewer.

items.p: Which two marks in human chromosome 2 show that it was once two chromosomes?
items.a: End letters in the middle of the chromosome, where no ends belong. And the faded remains of a second pinched-in place.
items.why: A joined chromosome keeps traces of the two old ends and of both pinched-in places. Both were found.

items.p: Learning something by watching others is called ____ learning.
items.why: Social learning is how traditions pass from one member of a group to another.

items.p: Put in order how scientists decide that a habit is culture.
a: List habits common in one group and missing in another
Remove the ones the place can explain
Remove the ones genes can explain
Call what is left learned culture
items.why: Culture is what remains after the place and genes are ruled out.
items: Remove the ones genes can explain
Call what is left learned culture
List habits common in one group and missing in another
Remove the ones the place can explain

items.p: One chimpanzee group cracks no nuts. Their forest has no nut trees. What causes this difference?
items.why: They cannot crack nuts that are not there. Choosing 'culture' skips the first check: could the place explain it?

items.p: Sort each difference by its cause: learned, the place, or genes.
items.a: see items
items.why: Ask two questions. Does the place offer the same things? Is the family the same? If both are yes, the difference is learned.
items: eating with chopsticks or with the hand
thick wool in Ladakh, cotton in Chennai
no termite fishing where there are no mounds

items.p: In the mirror test, what shows that an ape knows whose reflection it is?
opts: Touching the mark on their own face
items.why: The mark can be seen only in the mirror. Touching it on their own face shows the ape links the reflection to their own body. Looking behind the mirror suggests the ape expects another animal there.

items.p: A chimpanzee beat students at a glance memory test. Give one reason the comparison was not fully fair.
items.a: The chimpanzee had practised the task for years and the students had not. When people practised a lot, they matched him.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here both the species and the amount of practice differed.

items.p: True or false: '99 per cent the same DNA' counts every kind of difference.
items.why: False. It counts only single letters that differ where the two can be lined up. Stretches that are added or missing are left out.

items.p: Draw two chromosomes joined end to end. Mark the old ends and both pinched-in places.
items.a: One long chromosome with two end marks side by side in the middle, an end mark at each tip, and two pinched-in places, one in each half.
items.why: A strong drawing shows marks in the middle that a normal chromosome would not have.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each finding is something a watcher could see. The idea on the right is what the finding points to.
pairs: End letters in the middle of a chromosome
A habit spreads only to those who watched
Touching a dye mark seen in a mirror
Looking where someone wrongly expects a thing

items.p: Two children argue about how different humans and chimpanzees are.
items.a: A strong answer says both are right, because one gives the share and the other the count. It may add that small changes in DNA switches can have large effects.
items.why: 1.2 in 100 is a small share. It is also about 35 million letters. Which one you say depends on what you want to show.

views.says: Only 1 letter in 100 differs, so we are nearly the same.
That is 35 million letters, so we are very different.

items.ask: Who is right? Explain how both numbers can be true.

items.p: Why does a group of great apes recover slowly after losing some adults?
opts: Mothers have one baby every several years
Apes do not live in groups
Babies are born only in winter
items.why: A chimpanzee mother has a baby about every five years, and an orangutan about every seven or eight. Few young are born, so numbers rise slowly.

items.p: One new habit spread only to watchers. Another appeared in animals who watched nobody. Which shows social learning? Why?
items.a: The first. If only those who watched picked it up, then watching was needed. The second could be worked out alone.
items.why: To show social learning you must know who watched whom, and not only that a habit became common.

items.p: 'Only humans make tools' was believed until 1960. Why had nobody shown it wrong before then?
items.a: Nobody had watched wild apes closely for long enough. Wild chimpanzees ran from people, so short visits showed very little.
items.why: Not seeing something is weak evidence when few people have looked. The claim rested on a lack of watching.

items.p: A scientist writes 'not seen in other apes so far'. What does she mean?
opts: Apes do it only in secret
items.why: It reports what has been found up to now. Choosing 'can never' turns a gap in the evidence into a fact about apes.

items.p: Two scientists argue about the minds of humans and other apes.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For the first: tools, traditions and the mirror test were once called human-only. For the second: no other ape has grammar or culture that builds up.
items.why: This is still argued about. What matters is using evidence for your side and seeing the best point on the other.

views.says: The difference is one of amount. Other apes have smaller amounts of the same abilities.
There is a real gap. Some human abilities are new kinds of things.

items.ask: Which view fits the evidence better? Give one piece of evidence for your side and one for the other.

items.p: True or false: chimpanzees are an earlier, less evolved form of humans.
items.why: False. Both lines have been changing for the same length of time since they split. Evolution is a branching tree and not a ladder.

items.p: Children copy a step they can see is useless. Why might that habit be useful for humans?
items.a: Many human skills are too complicated to see why each step matters. Copying exactly keeps the steps that work, so skills can be passed on and built up.
items.why: This is one idea about how human culture builds up. It is not settled.

items.p: Young chimpanzees left out a step when they could see it did nothing. What does that show?
opts: They understood what the step did
items.why: With a box they could not see into, the chimpanzees did copy the step. With a clear box they skipped it. So they could copy, and chose not to.

items.p: Sort each claim about 'only humans' by what the evidence says.
items.a: see items
items.why: Tools and laughter have been seen in other apes. Grammar and teaching are argued about. Cooking and writing have not been seen.

items.p: We are equally related to chimpanzees and bonobos. Why can neither show what humans are 'naturally' like?
items.a: The two live very differently, one more violent and one more peaceful. Since we are as close to one as to the other, neither can be picked as the model for us.
items.why: Two equally close relatives who differ show that close relatives can go different ways.

items.p: What is cumulative culture?
opts: Skills that build up over generations
Any habit learned from a mother
A habit caused by the place
items.why: In cumulative culture each generation adds to what the last one knew. Choosing 'any habit learned' describes culture in general, which other apes have.

items.p: True or false: where people have changed forests most, chimpanzee groups show fewer learned traditions.
items.why: True. A 2019 study of 144 chimpanzee communities found this. Small, scattered groups give the young fewer chances to watch.

items.p: Draw a test of whether a crow will use a stick to reach food. Label what stays the same.
items.a: A drawing with food out of beak reach, such as in a tube, and sticks nearby. Labels say what stays the same each time: the tube, the food, the distance and the time allowed.
items.why: A strong design lets the crow show the skill without being taught, and keeps everything else the same.
items.art: A blank table top with an outline of a crow at one side.

items.p: Imagining human feelings in an animal when they may not be there is called ____.
items.why: Scientists guard against it by writing down what the animal does. They must also guard against the opposite mistake, which is refusing to see a feeling that is there.

items.p: Three of these have been seen in wild chimpanzees. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: No wild ape has been seen making or keeping fire. The other three are well-known chimpanzee tool uses.

items.p: Which is the best kind of guess in science?
opts: One that evidence could show wrong
One that fits whatever is found
items.why: The joined chromosome idea said what marks should be there. If they had been missing, the idea would have failed. A guess that fits anything tells us nothing.

items.p: 'Special' can mean 'different from others' or 'above others'. Which meaning can science test? Explain.
items.a: Science can test 'different', by comparing what each species does. It has no test for 'above', because that depends on what you choose to value.
items.why: A chimpanzee is better at glance memory and a human at language. Which matters more is a choice, not a measurement.

quiz.p: Which two apes are humans' closest living relatives?
quiz.why: Our line and the line of chimpanzees and bonobos split most recently. Macaques and langurs are monkeys.

opts: A being from whom two kinds both descend
The strongest member of a group
quiz.why: Two kinds of living beings today can both descend from one group long ago. No chimpanzee became human.

quiz.p: What does the join in human chromosome 2 explain?
opts: Why humans have 46 chromosomes and other great apes 48
quiz.why: Two ancestral chromosomes joined end to end on the human line. The same DNA is packed into one pair fewer.

quiz.p: True or false: there is one exact number for how alike human and chimpanzee DNA is.
quiz.why: False. Counting single letters gives almost 99 per cent. Counting added and missing stretches too gives about 96. The answer depends on what is counted.

quiz.p: A fishing stalk must pass through a narrow hole. Why strip the leaves first?
opts: Leaves catch on the edge of the hole
Leaves make the stalk too heavy
quiz.why: A termite tunnel is narrow. A bare stem slides in, and a leafy one jams. Stripping it is changing a thing to fit a job.

quiz.p: Chimpanzees fray a stem tip into a brush. Why does a brush catch more termites?
opts: More fibres for termites to hold on to
A brush is longer than a stem
quiz.why: Termites bite on to what enters the nest. Many fine fibres give them more to grip than one smooth end.

quiz.p: Two groups differ in a habit. Which finding points most strongly to culture?
opts: The habit spreads only to those who watch it
quiz.why: If only watchers pick the habit up, the habit is learned from others. A wetter forest would point to the place.

quiz.p: Which of these is a tradition?
opts: Cracking nuts the way your group does
quiz.why: A tradition is learned from others in the group. Eye colour is inherited, and growing and hunger happen without learning.

quiz.p: In a film test, an ape looks where a person wrongly thinks a ball is. What might this show?
opts: The ape tracks what the person believes
The ape cannot see the ball
quiz.why: The ape knows where the ball really is, yet looks where the person will search. That suggests the ape follows the person's belief. How far this goes is still argued about.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists agree that apes taught signs are using full language.
quiz.why: False. Apes have learned hundreds of signs. Whether they use grammar, which language needs, is still argued about.

quiz.p: Why did Jane Goodall see what earlier visitors had missed?
opts: She watched the same chimpanzees for years
She tested them in a laboratory
quiz.why: Wild chimpanzees hide from strangers. Only after months did they let her near enough to see tool making, and only years showed whole lives.

quiz.p: Which of these has not been seen in any wild ape other than humans?
quiz.why: No wild ape makes fire or cooks. The other three have been seen many times in chimpanzees.

applications: People who protect apes now plan to save whole groups and their traditions. An ape raised alone by people misses the years of watching that wild young apes get.
Good zoos and sanctuaries give apes puzzles, such as food hidden in tubes and logs, because a mind that makes tools needs problems to solve.
Because apes are so like us, people once used chimpanzees to test medicines. For the same reason, many countries have now stopped.
Scientists study ape gestures to work out how human language might have begun.
Rope and tree bridges across roads and railway lines let gibbons and other tree-living primates cross gaps in the forest.
Teachers use what is known about learning by watching. Showing a skill slowly, and letting the learner use your tool, is how many crafts are still taught.
Courts in some countries have had to decide whether an ape can have rights. The evidence in this lesson is what the judges were shown.

open_questions.q: Do other apes teach their young on purpose?
open_questions.why_open: There are only a few clear cases, and scientists do not agree on what should count as teaching.

open_questions.q: Why do chimpanzees and bonobos, who are so closely related, live so differently?
open_questions.why_open: Food, the absence of gorillas south of the Congo River and the bonds between females have all been suggested. Nobody has been able to test these ideas properly.

open_questions.q: Which DNA differences between humans and chimpanzees matter most?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the 35 million differing letters seem to change nothing. Finding the few that change how a brain or a body grows is slow work.

open_questions.q: Did human language begin with gestures like those of other apes?
open_questions.why_open: Gestures and words leave no fossils. Scientists compare living apes and babies, and the evidence can be read in more than one way.

open_questions.q: Did Rakus the orangutan work out his wound medicine alone, or learn it from others?
open_questions.why_open: It has been seen once, in one orangutan who was born somewhere else. Nobody has yet seen another orangutan do it.

open_questions.q: Is there anything in the human mind that is truly a new kind of thing?
open_questions.why_open: Every proposed difference has someone arguing that other apes have a small amount of it. The argument has gone on since Darwin.

Why do you think people liked the idea that only humans make tools?
A chimpanzee beats you at one memory test. What might you beat a chimpanzee at? Is either of you cleverer?
Would you rather be numbered or named by a scientist studying you? Why?
If apes grieve and comfort each other, should that change how people treat them?

maths.problem: In the Termite Fishing Test, a brush tip brought out 55 seeds in 5 dips. A stripped stalk brought out 25 in 5 dips. Find the average for each. How many times as many did the brush catch?
maths.answer: 11 seeds a dip for the brush and 5 for the stripped stalk. The brush caught 2.2 times as many.
maths.explain: 55 ÷ 5 = 11 seeds for each dip. 25 ÷ 5 = 5 seeds for each dip. 11 ÷ 5 = 2.2. So the brush tip caught a little more than twice as many.
maths.context: This is about the Termite Fishing Test. There you fish sesame seeds out of a covered tumbler with three kinds of stalk. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: total seeds in 5 dips

maths.why_maths: Saying 'how many times as many' compares two tools fairly, whatever the number of dips.

maths.problem: At real termite nests, brush tips brought out about 4.9 termites a try. Plain stems brought out about 0.27. About how many times better was the brush? Why might your seed test give a smaller number?
maths.answer: About 18 times better. Seeds only stick, but termites bite and hold on, so fibres matter more for termites.
maths.explain: 4.9 ÷ 0.27 is about 18. In the seed test the brush was about 2 times better. A model leaves things out. Sesame seeds stick to any wet surface. Live termites grip with their jaws, and a smooth stem gives them little to grip.
maths.context: This is about the Termite Fishing Test. There a covered tumbler of seeds stands for a termite mound. The termite numbers are from a real test in the Republic of Congo in 2009.
maths.why_maths: Comparing your number with the real one shows how good your model is, and what it leaves out.

maths.problem: One set of human DNA has about 3,000 million letters. About 1.2 letters in every 100 differ from a chimpanzee's. About how many letters is that?
maths.explain: 3,000 million ÷ 100 = 30 million. That is 1 in every 100. 30 million × 1.2 = 36 million. The 2005 study counted about 35 million.
maths.context: This is about The Hundred Square. There you colour boxes on a square of 100 to show how much human and chimpanzee DNA differ.
maths.why_maths: A share such as 1 in 100 sounds small. Multiplying shows the real count, which is very large.

maths.problem: People watched 20 films of ape gestures and chose 1 meaning out of 4 each time. How many would pure guessing get right? They got more than 10 right. What does that tell you?
maths.answer: Guessing would get about 5 right. More than 10 is twice that, so people were not just guessing.
maths.explain: With 4 choices, a guess is right 1 time in 4. 20 ÷ 4 = 5. A score above 10 is more than double what luck gives. So people really do understand many ape gestures.
maths.context: This is about Talking Without Words. There your family guesses messages from gestures alone. The numbers here are from a real online study in 2023.
maths.why_maths: You can only say a score is good if you know what luck alone would give. Working out the chance score gives you that line.

maths.problem: In the floating nut puzzle, 24 children of each age were tested. 8 per cent of four-year-olds, 42 per cent of six-year-olds and 58 per cent of eight-year-olds solved it. About how many children is that in each group? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: About 2, 10 and 14 children. More children solve it as they get older, but even at eight, 10 of the 24 did not.
maths.explain: 8 per cent of 24 is about 2. 42 per cent of 24 is about 10. 58 per cent of 24 is about 14. The number rises with age. All 5 orangutans solved it, which is 100 per cent.
maths.context: This is about The Nut in the Bottle. There you get a groundnut out of an upright bottle. These are real results from a study in 2011.
maths.why_maths: Turning percentages back into children shows how small the groups were, and makes the pattern with age easy to see.

maths.problem: In a Copycat Test, 3 of 4 people tapped the lid. What fraction is that? Could you now say that three quarters of all people copy useless steps? Why or why not?
maths.answer: Three quarters. No, because 4 people are far too few to speak for everyone.
maths.explain: 3 out of 4 is three quarters, or 75 per cent. But if one person had acted differently, the result would be 50 or 100 per cent. With so few people, one person changes everything. Scientists test many people before they say what most people do.
maths.context: This is about the Copycat Test. There you show people four steps for opening a clear box, two of them useless, and see what they copy. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A fraction from a small group looks exact but is not. Thinking about how one person shifts it shows how much to trust it.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that humans are not the only tool makers? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1960 scientists defined humans as 'Man the Toolmaker'. They held that only humans make tools. Nobody had watched wild apes for long enough to check. On 14 July 1960 Jane Goodall, aged 26, arrived at Gombe in Tanzania with her mother, Vanne. She had no university degree. For months the chimpanzees ran from her. She kept returning to the same hillside until they let her stay. That autumn she watched a male she called David Greybeard push a grass stem into a termite mound and eat the termites holding on to it. Soon she saw chimpanzees pick leafy twigs and strip the leaves off before fishing. They were making a tool. She sent word to Louis Leakey, the scientist who had sent her to Gombe. He replied: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Some scientists doubted a young woman with no training. Then the fishing was photographed and filmed, and watchers at other sites saw tool making too. The old definition was dropped.
how_we_found_out.who: Jane Goodall, an Englishwoman, with the chimpanzee David Greybeard. Louis Leakey sent her to Gombe, and her mother, Vanne Morris-Goodall, went with her.
how_we_found_out.when: She arrived on 14 July 1960. She saw the termite fishing in the autumn of that year.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That only humans make tools. It was shown wrong when someone watched wild chimpanzees every day for months and saw them strip twigs to fish for termites.
how_we_found_out.art: A young woman in khaki crouching behind tall grass with binoculars, watching a chimpanzee with a grey chin poke a stem into a red earth termite mound.

roots.context: We have learned what humans share with the other apes: DNA, bodies, tools, traditions and feelings. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Termite Fishing Test, you changed a stalk until it fitted the job. A chimpanzee named David Greybeard did the same in 1960. Until then, books said that making tools was what made us human. So that line between humans and other apes was drawn by people who had not yet watched. Each time someone has watched patiently, the line has had to move.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'humans and animals', as if there were a wall between the two with a list of human-only things on our side. The list was written before anyone had checked. It tells us more about what people wanted to be true than about apes.
deep_truth.evidence: Tool making came off the list in 1960 at Gombe. Culture came off when 39 learned traditions were counted in 1999, and when a moss sponge was filmed spreading in 2011. Knowing oneself in a mirror came off in 1970. In your own test, a frayed stalk caught more seeds than a plain one, as a frayed stem catches more termites for a chimpanzee.

three.who_am_i: You are a great ape. Your hands, your laugh, your long childhood and your habit of learning by watching are older than humans are.
three.what_is_life: Life does not come in ranks. It comes in branches. Each living kind has been changing for exactly as long as every other.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of other minds that make, learn, remember and care. Our closest cousins show this most clearly, because we can read their faces and hands.

roots.thread: About 6 to 8 million years ago there was one group of apes. From that group came chimpanzees, bonobos and us. Go further back and the same is true of gorillas, orangutans, gibbons, monkeys and every living being. The many kinds are one family that has branched. What we find in ourselves, such as making, learning from each other and caring, was not added to us from outside. It was already growing in that family before we were human.

teachings.teaching: All living beings are alike in birth. What sets them apart is what they do.
teachings.link: The Tamil words are 'ella uyirkkum', which means 'for all lives'. Many translators write 'all people'. Read in the wider way, the couplet says what this lesson found. We and the other apes begin from the same birth and the same family. The differences are in what each does.

teachings.teaching: The wise look with the same eye on a learned person, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a person whom others look down on.
teachings.link: The verse asks for one way of seeing across kinds of beings and across ranks among people. The science here removes the reasons people gave for ranking humans above the other apes.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, The Descent of Man (1871), summary at the end of the chapters that compare the minds of humans and other animals
teachings.teaching: Darwin wrote: 'the difference in mind between man and the higher animals, great as it is, certainly is one of degree and not of kind.'
teachings.link: Darwin wrote this ninety years before anyone had watched wild chimpanzees closely. Tools, traditions and the mirror test are the kind of evidence he expected.

science.text: Humans, chimpanzees and bonobos descend from common ancestors who lived about 6 to 8 million years ago. DNA and the joined chromosome 2 both show it.
Whether anything in the human mind is a new kind of ability, and not a larger amount of something other apes have, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Thomas Suddendorf, a psychologist who has studied children and other apes, in his book The Gap (2013)
other_view.view: He agrees that we are apes and that the old list was too long. But he argues that a real gap remains. Only humans imagine endless possible situations, tell each other about them, and build on what others have thought. He says we should study the gap honestly and not pretend it is not there.

practice.title: The hand you share
practice.say: Hold one hand open in front of you. Look at the nails, the lines on the palm and the tiny ridges on each fingertip. Touch your thumb slowly to each finger. A chimpanzee, a gorilla and an orangutan have all of these. This hand is older than humans are. Now close your eyes. Breathe in and out three times. Feel the hand from the inside.
practice.kid: Hold your hand open. Look at the nails, the lines and the fingertip ridges. Touch your thumb to each finger. Other apes have all of these too. Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Feel your hand from the inside.

ask: If the list of things that only humans do keeps getting shorter, what do you think will be left on it?
Why do you think people wanted humans to be separate from the other animals?
A chimpanzee is as closely related to you as to a bonobo. Does knowing that change how you see a chimpanzee?
When you look into the eyes of a dog, a crow or a monkey, do you think someone is looking back?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step for a city flat. They have not yet been tried at home. The Termite Fishing Test (core) needs three fresh curry-leaf stalks, a steel tumbler, paper, a rubber band and sesame seeds. Seeds stick only to a wet tip, so the step says to wet the tip before every dip. Expect the leafy stalk to bring out almost nothing, the stripped stalk a few seeds each dip and the brush tip the most. If the brush fibres stick together into one point, the brush may not win. The last step says what to look for then. If a stalk will not fray, the step gives a thread tip to use in its place. The Copycat Test needs at least three people who have not read the page, and with so few people the result can go either way. The step and one maths problem say so. The Nut in the Bottle spills water, so the bottle stands on a tray. A groundnut in the shell floats. Check that yours drops through the bottle neck before you start. Hammer and Anvil needs a grown-up close by, and is not for children with a groundnut allergy. The numbers in the made-up results agree across the experiments, the maths and the worksheets.
